items.title: Indonesia: Landmark Ruling Allows Civilian Trials of Soldiers
items.description: Click to expand Image The Constitutional Court of Indonesia, in Jakarta, October 2023. © 2023 Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images (London) – The Indonesian Constitutional Court’s ruling requiring reform of the military justice system so that military personnel accused of ordinary crimes can be tried in civilian courts is a major step for justice in Indonesia, Human Rights Watch said today. The government should immediately revise the 1997 Military Justice Law, which has long prevented civilian prosecutions of members of the armed forces for crimes under the Indonesian criminal code, including for serious human rights violations. On October 15, 2026, the Constitutional Court’s nine justices unanimously ruled that the Military Justice Law is conditionally unconstitutional under articles 24(1) and 28D(1) of the 1945 Constitution, which guarantee an independent judiciary and equality before the law. The law will become unconstitutional if it is not amended by October 2028, giving the government a two-year deadline. “The Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling recognizes that Indonesia’s military courts aren’t capable of impartially trying crimes against civilians, as victims and human rights defenders have said for decades, ” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “President Prabowo Subianto and the Indonesian parliament should consult with victims and rights groups and promptly amend the military justice law.” Under the 1997 law, civilian police cannot investigate military personnel, with only a few rarely invoked exceptions. Even when soldiers serving in civilian institutions have been accused of crimes under the criminal code, military courts have had jurisdiction over the case. Human Rights Watch found that Indonesia’s military justice system lacks transparency, independence, and impartiality, and has failed to properly investigate and prosecute alleged serious human rights abuses by military personnel. The petitioners challenged articles 9(1), 43(3), and 127 of the law, which allow active duty military personnel to be tried in military courts even for crimes ordinarily prosecuted in civilian courts. The Constitutional Court found that the distinction between military offenses and ordinary criminal offenses must be clearly defined. Justice Enny Nurbaningsih said that when an offense has no military character but accountability for it remains within a command-based system, “there is a structural risk that military’s institutional interests will conflict with the need to ensure independent and impartial legal proceedings.” The Constitutional Court also noted that the military judiciary is not fully integrated into the judicial system overseen by the Supreme Court and urged lawmakers to create a single system. Military judges are active duty soldiers, and investigation, prosecution, and adjudication all take place within the military chain-of-command. Revisions to the Military Justice Law have been pending for decades. As part of structural reforms that followed the end of authoritarian rule under President Soeharto from 1965 to 1998, the 2004 Armed Forces Law made soldiers subject to civilian courts for ordinary crimes. However, that provision would only take effect when a new military justice law was enacted. The Constitutional Court’s ruling imposes a two-year time frame for those revisions, which successive Indonesian governments have deferred. Muhammad Afif Abdul Qoyim, a lawyer from the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, told Human Rights Watch: “There is no need to wait two years to revise the Law on Military Justice so that new rules are in line with the Constitutional Court’s ruling.” Serious abuses by Indonesian security forces have gone unpunished for decades because of legal restrictions on civilian investigations and prosecutions under the 1997 law, Human Rights Watch said. On March 12, 2026, military personnel carried out an acid attack against Andrie Yunus, a 27-year-old deputy coordinator at KontraS (Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence), causing burns over 24 percent of his body and possible loss of sight in his right eye. A military court in Jakarta convicted four soldiers in June and sentenced them to 18 months to three years in prison and dismissal from the military. On August 20, a military appeals court reduced the two longest sentences by six months each and overturned their dishonorable discharges. The Judicial Commission has alleged ethical violations by the panel that tried the case at first instance. KontraS said in a statement that the Constitutional Court ruling “closes a legal loophole that has been seen as shielding errant soldiers from accountable law enforcement, and marks a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and completing the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia.” One of the petitioners in the case is the mother of a 15-year-old boy tortured to death in Medan, North Sumatra, in 2024 by a soldier who was sentenced by a military court to only 10 months in prison, though the maximum penalty is 15 years. In Papua, the military justice system has repeatedly failed victims of violence allegedly committed by military personnel. Under President Prabowo Subianto, a former general dismissed from the military for human rights violations, the military’s role in civilian affairs has expanded. In March 2025, the national legislature passed amendments to the Armed Forces Law to allow active duty officers to hold more government posts. The number of civilian institutions open to serving soldiers—which includes the Supreme Court and the Attorney General’s office—rose from 10 to 14. Lawmakers should prioritize amending the Military Justice Law through an open process with meaningful participation of victims and civil society, Human Rights Watch said. The amended law should clarify investigative and prosecutorial powers and provide a mechanism for transferring cases from military courts to the civilian system. “Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” Pearson said. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”

items.title: Niger: Prominent Journalist ‘Disappeared’ for 2 Months
items.description: Click to expand Image Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, former correspondent for Radio France Internationale, February 12, 2007. © 2007 Seyllou/AFP via Getty Images (Nairobi) – Niger’s authorities should urgently disclose the whereabouts of the prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who was forcibly disappeared two months ago, Human Rights Watch said today. They should ensure his safety and release him unless he has been charged with a valid criminal offense. On August 31, 2026, Kaka, the director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former correspondent for Radio France Internationale (RFI), left his office in Niamey, the capital, to return home but never arrived, raising immediate concerns. For weeks, his family and colleagues were not able to obtain information about his whereabouts. On September 25, during Niger’s Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva, Justice Minister Alio Daouda acknowledged that Kaka was being detained. The minister said Kaka was being held for an alleged “offense” and would “answer before the courts,” but provided no details about the accusation or his place of detention. “Two months after Moussa Kaka vanished in Niger, the authorities have yet to provide his location or explain his detention,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Kaka’s family will continue to grapple with the uncertainty until the authorities resolve his disappearance.” Kaka is a respected figure in African investigative journalism. For years, he reported for RFI in Niger, until the military junta suspended its broadcasts in 2023. Throughout his career, he has continued his work under successive governments despite the risks and repeated detentions for his journalism. In September 2007, under then-President Mamadou Tandja, the authorities arrested Kaka and accused him of links to ethnic Tuareg rebels, following his extended coverage of the Tuareg rebellion in northern Niger. He spent 379 days in prison before being released in October 2008 following a sustained national and international campaign for his freedom. In October 2025, police in Niamey arrested Kaka along with five other journalists after they announced on social media a press briefing about a government-created solidarity fund intended to support the country’s security forces. The journalists were charged with “complicity in distributing documents likely to disturb public order” under Niger’s broad cybercrime law. All six were subsequently released. Kaka’s recent forced disappearance came amid heightened political tensions following an attempted military coup in Niamey on August 29. After mutinous soldiers attempted to seize power, the junta arrested dozens of suspected soldiers and a former minister. Russian government-controlled Africa Corps forces were called upon to help suppress the mutiny. Kaka’s colleagues and friends have expressed concern that his disappearance may be linked to the junta’s crackdown after the attempted coup. Reporters Without Borders has referred Kaka’s case to the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances, following an earlier referral to the African Union’s special rapporteur on freedom of expression and access to information. African civil society organizations raised his case at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights in mid-October in Dakar, Senegal. Journalists and human rights activists across Africa have also called for his release. “Moussa Kaka’s place is not in detention,” said Alioune Tine, a prominent Senegalese human rights defender and former UN rights expert. “His detention is absolutely unjustified and violates Niger’s international human rights obligations, including provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which Niger has signed and ratified.” Kaka’s case highlights growing concerns about media freedom and political repression in Niger, Human Rights Watch said. Since seizing power in a 2023 coup, Niger’s military junta has solidified its rule, dismantled democratic institutions, and intensified repression of dissidents. They have dissolved political parties, suspended dozens of civil society organizations, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, stripped exiled political opponents of their nationality, announced the country’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and extended the political transition without holding elections. The authorities also continue to arbitrarily detain former President Mohamed Bazoum and his wife, and a prominent human rights defender, Moussa Tiangari. Under international human rights law, an enforced disappearance occurs when state agents, or people acting with the state’s authorization, support, or acquiescence, deprive someone of their liberty and then refuse to acknowledge the detention or conceal the person’s fate or whereabouts. Enforced disappearance places victims at heightened risk of torture and extrajudicial execution. It also inflicts profound suffering on families, who are left uncertain whether their loved ones are alive or dead and denied access to justice. “Niger’s authorities should immediately account for Kaka and free him if he hasn’t been fairly charged,” Allegrozzi said. “Governments and international organizations should press the junta to take immediate action in Kaka’s case.”

items.title: Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale : les partenaires sociaux de Solenzo informés et sensibilisés
items.description: Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Solenzo, Marou Ilboudo, a présidé le séminaire régional d’information et de sensibilisation des assurés sociaux de Bankui-Sourou de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), le jeudi 22 octobre 2026 à Solenzo. La direction régionale de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS) de Bankui et du Sourou s’est déportée à Solenzo, chef-lieu de la province des Banwa, le jeudi 22 octobre 2026. C’était dans le cadre de son séminaire régional d’information et de sensibilisation des partenaires sociaux au sujet de la sécurité sociale. La rencontre a réuni des responsables d’entreprises, des employeurs et des employés, des représentants des directions générale et régionale de la CNSS et des présidents d’associations. L’occasion a été donnée aux usagers de s’informer sur les missions de la caisse à travers, entre autres, ses prestations fournies, les cotisations sociales, les moda-lités d’affiliation et le cadre juridique sous lequel elle opère. Le directeur régional de la CNSS Dédougou, Wendmalgré Sawadogo, a indiqué que selon la loi portant régime de sécurité sociale au Burkina Faso, la sécurité sociale s’affirme plus que jamais comme un pilier essentiel de la cohésion nationale, de progrès économique et de justice sociale. Il a expliqué qu’elle protège les travailleurs contre les aléas de la vie à savoir les maladies, les accidents de travail, l’invalidité, la vieillesse et la perte d’un soutien de la famille. « C’est pour répondre à ces exigences que la CNSS s’est engagée dans un processus continu de modernisation, de rapprochement avec les usagers, l’amélioration de la qualité de ses prestations, la mission d’informer, de former et de sensibiliser les partenaires sociaux à leurs droits et obligations, gage d’une sécurité sociale inclusive et fiable », a affirmé M. Sawadogo. Le présent séminaire, a-t-il dit, s’inscrit dans cette perspective. Les préoccupations recueillies auprès des participants sont, entre autres, relatives à la nécessité de rapprocher la CNSS de ses assurés de la province des Banwa, aux difficultés liées à l’effectivité des cotisations sociales par les employeurs et à la mise en œuvre de certaines décisions de justice favorables aux travailleurs. Satisfaction des partenaires Les organisateurs de l’activité ont apporté des réponses aux interrogations soulevées par les bénéficiaires du séminaire. Ces derniers ont apprécié la démarche de la caisse. Laurence Douanio a dit avoir découvert que la caisse offre des possibilités d’aide aux femmes pendant les congés de maternité. Pour Daouda Kané, c’est désormais clair pour lui que chaque employeur doit déclarer ses employés et verser régulièrement à bonne date les cotisations sociales de ceux-ci à la caisse de sécurité sociale. « L’employé doit aussi veiller à ce que sa situation soit régularisée à la caisse si son patron ne l’a pas fait », a-t-il renchéri. Le directeur régional des serviteurs du peuple de Bankui, Djissié Sougué, a salué l’organisation de cette activité qui offre le cadre de porter l’information utile aux usagers. Il a exhorté les acteurs à s’inscrire dans les directives tracées par la CNSS en matière de sécurité sociale. Il a relevé que les droits des travailleurs sont, parmi tant d’autres, la pension de retraite, l’allocation familiale ou prénatale et les risques professionnels. A côté de ses droits, il y a les devoirs, a-t-il sonné, comme un rappel. Le chef du service de recouvrement à la CNSS au niveau central, Abdoul Aziz Bado, a insisté sur le respect des délais dans le paiement des cotisations sociales par les patrons sous peine de pénalité après l’expiration des délais de grâce qui sont de 15 jours pour la cotisation mensuelle et de 30 jours pour celle trimestrielle. Le président de la délégation spéciale de Solenzo, Marou Ilboudo, dira que la CNSS est le pilier central du système de prévoyance sociale avec pour « mission fondamentale de payer les droits des assurés sociaux sur la base d’un recouvrement optimum des cotisations sociales ». Et pour atteindre ses objectifs, elle s’investit dans l’élévation du niveau de compréhension de ses partenaires, a-t-il conclu. Yacouba BELEM

items.title: Burkina/Lutte contre le VIH-Sida : Une prévalence à 0,5 % et un nouveau plan stratégique pour intensifier la riposte
items.description: La 23ᵉ session ordinaire du Conseil national de lutte contre le sida et les infections sexuellement transmissibles (CNLS-IST) s'est tenue ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026. La cérémonie d'ouverture et les travaux ont été présidés par le ministre directeur de cabinet, le capitaine Martha Anderson Meda, représentant le président du Faso, président du CNLS-IST. La présente session a servi de cadre pour examiner l'état de mise en œuvre des recommandations et engagements de la 22ᵉ session, le bilan annuel du Plan national multisectoriel de lutte contre le VIH et les IST et valider le Plan stratégique national contre le VIH, le Sida et les IST pour la période 2026-2030. Au cours de l'année 2025, les actions menées par les acteurs publics et privés dans le cadre de la riposte ont permis de maintenir la prévalence du VIH à 0,5 % en population générale. Selon les données présentées par le capitaine Martha Anderson Meda, 87 534 personnes bénéficient d'un traitement antirétroviral et 93 % des personnes vivant avec le VIH connaissent leur statut sérologique. En matière de prévention de la transmission du VIH de la mère à l'enfant, 95,4 % des femmes enceintes reçues en consultation prénatale ont été dépistées. La quasi-totalité de celles dont le test s'est révélé positif (0,57 %) ont également été mises sous traitement. Ces résultats sont le fruit de l'engagement des différents acteurs, de la gratuité des soins et du suivi biologique, ainsi que de la décentralisation de la prise en charge. Le capitaine Martha Anderson Meda a présidé les travaux de la 23ᵉ session du CNLS-IST En 2025, le nombre de personnes vivant avec le VIH est estimé à 91 000, dont 5 800 enfants avec 1 600 nouvelles infections et 1 800 décès. Les statistiques indiquent que seuls 29% des enfants vivant avec le VIH sont identifiés et sous traitement, et 19% ont une charge virale supprimée. Les régions les plus touchées sont le Kadiogo 1,30%, le Nakambé 0,65%, le Guiriko 0,64%, le Nando 0,63% et l'Oubri 0,62%. Si les acquis en matière de lutte contre le sida et les IST sont indéniables, il n'en demeure pas moins que plusieurs défis pourraient compromettre l'objectif de mettre fin à la maladie en tant que menace de santé publique à l'horizon 2030. Le capitaine Anderson Meda a relevé cinq défis majeurs qu'il faille relever pour faire de l'élimination du VIH-Sida une réalité en 2030. Le premier défi concerne la suppression de la charge virale. En effet, seulement 61 % des personnes vivant avec le VIH ont une charge virale supprimée. L'amélioration de l'accès aux examens de suivi et à une prise en charge adaptée demeure donc un enjeu important. La prise en charge des enfants constitue le deuxième défi. Le dépistage et le traitement des enfants vivant avec le VIH restent insuffisants. L'exécution du plan d'urgence consacré au VIH pédiatrique doit donc être une priorité. Le troisième défi porte sur le renforcement de la prévention auprès des populations les plus exposées, notamment les travailleuses du sexe, les adolescents, les jeunes, les personnes déplacées internes ainsi que les forces de défense et de sécurité et les VDP. Selon le secrétaire permanent du CNLS-IST, plusieurs recommandations ont été formulées par les participants La résistance aux traitements chez certains patients représente également une préoccupation. Elle menace l'efficacité de la prise en charge et nécessite des mesures adaptées. Le cinquième défi est celui du financement. Seulement 59,41% des besoins du Plan national multisectoriel de lutte contre le VIH pour 2025 ont été couverts contre 71,43% en 2024. Le Plan stratégique national de lutte contre le VIH, le sida et les IST pour intensifier la lutte Pour répondre à ces difficultés, le Burkina Faso entend s'appuyer sur son nouveau Plan stratégique national de lutte contre le VIH, le sida et les IST pour la période 2026-2030. Soumis à la validation des membres du CNLS-IST, ce nouveau référentiel en matière de lutte contre le VIH/sida vise quatre objectifs. Ce sont la réduction de 95% des nouvelles infections, la réduction de 95% de la mortalité liée au VIH et aux comorbidités, l'amélioration de la qualité de vie de 95% des PV-VIH, des orphelins et enfants vulnérables, des populations à risque et enfin la mise en place de systèmes de gouvernance robustes et pérennes. Ce nouveau plan prévoit également une meilleure priorisation des interventions en fonction des populations et des régions, une intégration accrue des services de lutte contre le VIH dans le système de santé et un renforcement de l'appropriation nationale de la réponse à l'épidémie. Les partenaires techniques et financiers, par la voix du représentant résident de la FAO, Ernest Moïse Mushekuru, ont réaffirmé leur engagement à accompagner le gouvernement Pour sa mise en œuvre qui va nécessiter 138,12 milliards de FCFA, l'État s'est engagé à apporter au moins 50 % du financement. Il entend notamment honorer ses engagements auprès du Fonds mondial, afin de préserver la gratuité des traitements et des examens de suivi biologique, tout en augmentant progressivement les ressources nationales consacrées à la lutte contre le VIH. Le plan a été validé à l'unanimité par les membres du conseil présents à la session. À la fin de la 23ᵉ session, les membres du CNLS-IST ont fait un ensemble de recommandations. Selon le secrétaire permanent du CNLS-IST, il s'agit de renforcer les approches différenciées des prestations de services pour atteindre les objectifs 3x95 afin de progresser vers l'élimination du SIDA d'ici 2030, d'intensifier les dépistages précoces chez les enfants et de renforcer la prise en charge pédiatrique en garantissant un accès équitable au traitement antirétroviral. La troisième recommandation porte sur la prise en compte des besoins spécifiques des populations touchées par la crise, notamment les personnes déplacées internes et retournées, afin qu'une personne ne soit laissée de côté, et la quatrième sur le renforcement de la collaboration entre acteurs, pour aligner les interventions sur les priorités nationales et mobiliser les ressources nécessaires pour éliminer le VIH comme menace de santé publique d'ici 2030. Photo de famille Au cours de la session, les partenaires techniques et financiers, par la voix du représentant résident de la FAO, Ernest Moïse Mushekuru, ont réaffirmé leur engagement à accompagner le gouvernement, notamment dans le renforcement des approches différenciées et du VIH pédiatrique. Les acteurs engagés dans la lutte contre le VIH-SIDA et les IST ont aussi livré des messages de renouvellement de leur engagement et fait des plaidoyers pour l'amélioration des moyens mis à leur disposition dans le cadre de la lutte. items.title: Donald Trump annonce un sommet Poutine-Zelensky "très bientôt" sous médiation américaine
items.description: Le président américain, Donald Trump, a annoncé mercredi qu'une rencontre au sommet entre les présidents russe Vladimir Poutine et ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky serait organisée « très bientôt » sous médiation américaine. « Une rencontre sera organisée très bientôt et je pense que nous pourrions accomplir de grands progrès », a déclaré le locataire de la Maison-Blanche à des journalistes à bord de l'avion présidentiel Air Force One, alors qu’il rentrait d'un déplacement au Texas pour rejoindre Washington. Le chef de l’exécutif américain a affiché son optimisme, affirmant que ce tête-à-tête direct permettrait d’avancer vers une résolution de la guerre qui secoue l'Europe orientale. Bien que les modalités précises restent à formaliser, les premières lignes directrices de cette initiative diplomatique commencent à se dessiner. Zelensky avait indiqué dimanche qu'une réunion entre Russes et Ukrainiens aurait lieu en novembre sous médiation américaine pour relancer des négociations de paix au point mort depuis le début de l'année. La Russie avait annoncé deux jours auparavant qu'une telle réunion était prévue en novembre dans le cadre de récents efforts américains visant à réanimer les pourparlers de paix. items.title: Trump Is Closing From Behind
items.description: M odern political history offers few examples of closing arguments that appear more out of touch, self-defeating, or downright bizarre than what Donald Trump has offered his fellow Republicans ahead of next week’s midterm elections. In 1980, when Ronald Reagan told voters to consider Jimmy Carter’s presidency and ask themselves, “Are you better off than you were four years ago?,” it helped turn a tight race into a Reagan landslide. But many stretch-run messages prove deeply ineffective and are quickly forgotten. Ahead of the 1998 midterms, Republicans went all in on investigations that led to the impeachment of President Bill Clinton only to be rebuked by voters. President Obama’s insistence in 2010 that the country was coming out of the financial crisis led to his party enduring a “shellacking.” And during the 2018 midterms, Trump and his fellow Republicans tried to stoke fears about an alleged caravan of migrants headed toward the United States, only to have skeptical voters hand the House of Representatives to Democrats. This time around, Trump’s primary rationale for why voters should support the GOP, as best I can tell, is that the affordability crisis is a “hoax,” Bill Maher is a “loser,” and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a nice physique. That easy-to-mock message has been accompanied by a staggering number of missteps. Just for starters, he’s belittled the impact of his stalled war with Iran, sided with Russia as it continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, defended an attack ad from the GOP candidate for Ohio governor that repulsed other top Republicans, downplayed high energy prices while boasting that U.S. oil and gas companies are “making a freaking fortune,” embraced AI as the nation turns against it, obsessed over White House construction projects, and spent a lot of time talking about handsome men, Husted being just one. Many Republicans, and even some in Trump’s orbit, don’t quite get it. What has happened, they ask, to the instincts of the man who authored two of the most improbable victories in American political history? Trump’s superpower was his intuitive understanding of what motivated his supporters. Many Republicans privately tell me that he’s lost that feel. Trump now lives, they think, in a gilded bubble, palling around with billionaires, oblivious to—and, even worse, uncaring about—the problems facing so many voters. His approval rating has slipped to the low 30s. He’s become so toxic that some Republicans in tight races don’t want him anywhere near their state or congressional district, believing his rallies will harm more than help. Strategists in both parties expect Democrats to take control of the House, while the Senate is a true toss-up —a stunning reversal from the beginning of the year, when the upper chamber’s map looked so favorable for Republicans, and Trump cut a dominant figure. Suddenly, Republicans find themselves fighting to keep Senate seats in deep-red states: Kansas. Alaska. South Carolina. Ohio. Iowa. Mississippi. Texas. Trump is campaigning across the country, imploring his supporters to turn out for him one last time. But he’s given Republicans next to nothing to run on, and polls show that voters believe his economic policies are failing, his deportation program has gone too far, and his war is misguided. He instead has leaned hard on the political battles of the past, reheating fears about transgender surgeries (from his 2024 campaign), Muslim terrorists (all the way back to 2016), and even communism. (The guy does have a fondness for the ’80s .) For good measure, Trump’s Department of Justice charged the former FBI Director James Comey for a third time—the first two didn’t stick—because nothing screams being in tune with the everyday concerns of voters than trying to revive a faltering retribution campaign against a political foe your administration once targeted over a photograph of seashells. One Republican up for reelection who would speak with me only on the condition of anonymity, so as not to alienate the president, put it succinctly: “We may have lost the plot here.” N ot that long ago, the president was tossing Trump 2028 hats around, and Democrats were freaking out that he might be powerful enough to defy the Constitution. But that headgear now seems dated, as does the apparel line trumpeting that Trump Was Right About Everything! Many Republicans tell me that their party’s biggest problem just days from the election is that voters feel like Trump hasn’t kept his core promises. End foreign wars? Nope, there’s a new one in Iran that’s sent gas prices up and depleted the U.S. munitions supply. Plus, Trump has appeared to side with Russia over Ukraine in a conflict he once promised to end in 24 hours. Bring prices down? Well, the war in the Middle East has made that impossible, as have Trump’s haphazard trade wars, including tariffs on once-friendly trading partners such as Canada and the European Union. And while many Americans are struggling, Trump and his family are growing exponentially wealthier. Deport the worst of the worst? Trump’s massive roundups are targeting not just violent criminals or gang members, but also longtime community members, neighbors, parishioners, teammates, and friends with no criminal records. Many Americans have been horrified by the violence unleashed by masked federal agents, especially the killing of two U.S. citizens in the streets of Minneapolis. [ Read: Trump’s gamble to end the Iran war ] That Trump wants to focus on anything other than these broken promises while out on the campaign trail is perhaps unsurprising. At his Monday rally in Corinth, Mississippi, he spent seven minutes—nearly 10 percent of his entire speech—discussing his efforts to redecorate the White House. The day before—when Trump traveled to a rally in Port Huron, Michigan—the president’s talking points included faulting President Biden for the war in Ukraine; falsely claiming that more oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz than before the war; deeming Norway a “shithouse country”; calling Abdul El-Sayed, the state’s Democratic nominee for Senate, a jihadist (five times); saying that, should he win, El-Sayed will be the only senator who must go through a metal detector to get to work; comparing a vote against El-Sayed to stopping a deadly terror attack; asking the Trinidadian rapper Nicki Minaj to stand before thousands of his supporters so that they could appreciate her butt; and lauding the boulder-like shoulders, thick fingers, massive feet, and firm backside of (who else?) Husted, his preferred candidate for Senate in a different state. Over the course of that day, he spent three and a half minutes talking about Husted’s football career, which is three and a half minutes more than he talked about the lawmaker’s policies. Rather than dispel the notion that he has lost sight of what actually matters to voters, Trump on Sunday night released a social-media screed of more than 1,300 words (his longest Truth Social post ever) that assailed Maher for being ungrateful after the president hosted the comedian and talk-show host at the White House for dinner. The president has also fumed that Obama said over the weekend that Trump’s new White House decor is “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump angrily complained about the dig multiple times just yesterday. [ Read: Leave the Cheesecake Factory out of this ] Trump has also found himself on the wrong side of the day’s top issues. He misses few chances to mock the affordability crisis. Republicans and Democrats alike have swiftly turned on artificial intelligence, blasting the industry’s data centers as loud and expensive, and warning voters that the rapidly developing technology could take away their jobs or even their lives . Yet Trump has refused to regulate AI, knowing that the industry is propping up the stock market. His only nod toward change is trying to rename it “Super Intelligence.” Last week, Trump loudly supported a controversial ad from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor. The video features the estranged mother of the Democratic nominee Amy Acton, Donna Arthur, who accuses her daughter of lying about her past. It doesn’t mention that the two women have not spoken for decades, after the candidate’s stepfather was indicted for molesting her. The backlash was fierce and bipartisan; the state’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine, denounced the ad and demanded that it be pulled. Trump not only supported it but also urged Ramaswamy to “say thank you, God, very much” for such political good fortune. Divine intervention or not, several GOP strategists believe the ad could doom Ramaswamy. Some GOP candidates in tight races—Susan Collins in Maine, John Sununu in New Hampshire—have sent word to the White House that Trump isn’t welcome to campaign alongside them. The president has instead been dispatched to deep-red states with the hopes of turning out enough of his die-hard supporters to avoid losing once-safe Senate seats. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, insisted to me in a statement that Trump is remaining focused while “crisscrossing the country with unmatched energy and enthusiasm to deliver a simple message: with Republicans in control of Congress, Americans can expect safer streets, lower taxes, a secure border, and energy dominance.” T he most eyebrow-raising October surprise has been Trump’s unfiltered and rather randy assessments of the male form . His motivations remain a mystery, but some in the president’s circle have theories. One outside adviser who is close to the president told me that it began when Trump, while rallying for Husted two weeks ago, was first told that the senator had played college football in the late ’80s. Trump was impressed and began publicly ruminating over the next few days about Husted’s physique, including declaring that the senator’s “ass is like a pile of muscle.” That admiration quickly became a subject of interest on social media and cable shows, some of which resurfaced clips of Trump praising the good looks of Secret Service agents, generals, and a quarterback for the New York Giants. All of that prompted amused chatter about the 80-year-old president. But Trump has always been keenly interested in appearances, female or male, and has long made hiring decisions based on wanting looks out of “central casting.” As that adviser noted to me, Trump has spent decades in the public eye, obsessing about how his tan or hair looked on television; he’s given a lot of thought to his own appearance, so it’s not surprising that he’d think about how others look, too. [ Read: A different kind of fading president ] What is more surprising to many around Trump is just how freely he is expressing those thoughts. Any filter appears to be long gone. Then again, there may be simpler explanations: Once the Husted comments went viral, Trump’s rally crowds have come to expect the lines and have begun to laugh along, reinforcing the president’s sense that the material is working. And Trump would rather discuss almost anything besides the price of gas—even Husted’s posterior. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed research to this report.

items.title: ALTON urges states to scrap telecoms right-of-way fees
items.description: Association says charges account for up to 60% of fibre deployment costs By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja The Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria (ALTON) has urged state governments to abolish right-of-way charges on telecommunications infrastructure, warning that the fees account for up to 60 per cent of fibre-optic deployment costs in some states and discourage network expansion into underserved communities. The association said scrapping the charges, particularly in rural areas and locations with limited commercial prospects, would lower infrastructure deployment costs, attract investment and help bridge Nigeria’s digital divide. ALTON Chairman, Engr. Gbenga Adebayo, made the call on Tuesday on the sidelines of a plenary session sponsored by IHS Nigeria at the 2026 Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja. Right-of-way charges are fees imposed for permission to access and use public or private land, roads and other designated spaces to install fibre-optic cables and related telecommunications infrastructure. Adebayo said the high cost of obtaining right-of-way approvals had become a major obstacle to fibre deployment, making it difficult for operators to justify investments in communities where anticipated revenue might not cover infrastructure costs. “Today, the cost of right-of-way amounts to a significant part of the cost of fibre deployment. For every one kilometre of fibre that you deploy, in some of the states, the cost of right-of-way can be as high as 50 to 60 per cent of the cost of deploying the entire infrastructure,” he said. He called for legislation to make right-of-way access for telecommunications infrastructure free, particularly in rural communities and other areas where expected commercial returns were unlikely to attract private investment. According to him, removing the charges would make network expansion more affordable and encourage operators to extend services to communities with poor or no connectivity. The ALTON chairman also urged the government to introduce incentives for telecommunications companies investing in areas where infrastructure deployment costs exceeded the revenue they could reasonably expect to generate. He said existing government intervention mechanisms, particularly the Universal Service Provision Fund (USPF), could be deployed more strategically to support network expansion in underserved locations. “There are also intervention funds. We have the Universal Service Provision Fund, which is designed for special intervention in those areas that are lacking coverage,” Adebayo said. He dismissed suggestions that telecommunications operators were unwilling to invest in rural communities, arguing that the challenge was largely economic and could be addressed through appropriate incentives and targeted government support. Beyond expanding network coverage, Adebayo stressed the need for increased investment in fibre-optic cables, telecommunications sites and network capacity to improve service quality and prepare Nigeria for emerging technologies. He said artificial intelligence (AI) depended not only on software and computing power but also on the telecommunications infrastructure needed to support reliable connectivity and the transmission of large volumes of data. Describing telecommunications infrastructure as fundamental to the digital economy, he called for stronger investor participation to address the sector’s infrastructure needs and support Nigeria’s technological development. Meanwhile, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Shuaib Salisu, disclosed that the National Digital Economy and E-Government Bill had reached its third reading, expressing optimism that the National Assembly would pass it before the end of 2026. Salisu said lawmakers were also working on cybersecurity reforms and reviewing the Data Protection Act to strengthen Nigeria’s digital governance framework. He said the Federal Government’s planned 90,000-kilometre fibre-optic network would help extend connectivity to underserved communities and complement efforts to improve access to digital services. The senator also identified the Three Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme as a key initiative for developing the skilled workforce needed to support Nigeria’s growing digital economy. He urged businesses and industry stakeholders to engage lawmakers early in the legislative process, saying such engagement would help ensure that proposed laws reflected industry realities and the requirements for attracting investment. Also speaking at the summit, the Chargé d’Affaires of the United States Mission in Abuja, Jimmy Mauldin, called for stronger investment partnerships between Nigeria and the United States, stressing that cooperation should extend beyond trade to include job creation, technology transfer and support for local businesses. Mauldin identified digital infrastructure, energy, manufacturing, agriculture, critical minerals and financial services as sectors offering significant opportunities for deeper economic collaboration between the two countries. He said Nigeria’s large youthful population, growing technology sector and strategic position in West African commerce made it an attractive investment destination. However, he stressed that predictable government policies, respect for contracts, efficient trade procedures and improved security were essential to sustaining investor confidence and attracting long-term capital. “Capital is mobile. And it’s also important to remember that capital is very selective,” he said. Mauldin added that reliable electricity and secure communities were necessary for businesses to establish factories, deploy fibre-optic networks and operate efficient supply chains. The summit brought together government officials, business leaders, policymakers and development partners to examine investment opportunities, infrastructure development and strategies for accelerating Nigeria’s economic growth. items.title: A Stress Test for Prediction Markets
items.description: Sign up for Over/Under , a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk. Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, was reelected on Sunday night. Not everyone saw it coming. For weeks, many U.S. pundits had been suggesting that he would lose, thanks to the growing power of the South American right and the lingering curse of incumbency . This thesis was also plainly supported by recent Brazilian election data: Lula’s main opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro (son of Jair), had won the first round of the election, in early October, by more than 2 million votes, and subsequent polling consistently showed that the right-wing challenger had a slight edge. On both Kalshi and Polymarket , Bolsonaro’s odds of victory were bouncing within the mid-70- and high-80-percent range since the first round—more than a slight edge. Traders were betting on Bolsonaro across markets, even when, in the final days of the race, polling showed Lula gaining ground . That divergence between the prediction markets and the polls has led to some discussion about whether the markets can be trusted. It’s a critique that keeps coming up: Polymarket traders gave Francesca Hong, a candidate for the Wisconsin governorship, about a 95 percent chance of winning her August primary—right up until the day she lost. But these platforms deal in probabilities, and economists tend to advise against drawing conclusions from a sample size of one. Maybe Lula really did have a one-in-five chance of winning, as the prediction markets suggested, and maybe this was the one-in-five outcome. In industry parlance, probabilistic forecasts are said to be well “calibrated” if their odds correspond with the frequency of actual outcomes, and prediction markets do tend to be well calibrated . But in the case of Brazil, the markets heavily favored the candidate who didn’t win. That’s the technical explanation, anyway. The problem is that Kalshi and Polymarket have taken great pains to establish themselves as authoritative election forecasters . Both platforms are now running midterms “hubs,” where traders and observers can find data for the upcoming U.S. elections on a single page. Even outside of politics, these executives have consistently pushed the idea that they are running predictive platforms— prediction is in the name, after all. Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan has said that these markets are “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now, until someone else creates some sort of a super crystal ball.” This leaves some rhetorical wiggle room—the markets are not crystal balls—but it also sets an expectation of decisiveness and reliability. When the odds don’t appear to align with the outcomes, these firms can conveniently retreat to the fact that they’re purely dealing in probabilities. This argument is available to them as long as their forecasts don’t read zero percent or 100 percent. Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour told me yesterday that the “strong drag” toward Bolsonaro may have had to do with Brazil’s electoral history; traders could have been hung up on the fact that a presidential candidate had never lost after winning the first round. Still, the “market priced 20% chance of whatever happened to happen,” he said. Partly because of how prediction markets advertise themselves, some observers now ascribe them a predictive power that’s similar to polling, or to hybrid forecasts such as Decision Desk HQ, which gathers data from a variety of sources. But there are fundamental differences. Sophisticated polls are a snapshot of a moment in time—a representative sampling of people indicating how they plan to vote. Prediction markets, meanwhile, derive their probabilities from the trading data of users across the world. The kinds of people who typically use these platforms are mostly young and mostly male. Kalshi and Polymarket are banned in Brazil. Is it possible that traders without much knowledge of Brazilian politics, or who had their own political biases, skewed the results? In this case, it’s hard to know. Recent academic research suggests that prediction markets are still pretty good at producing reliable forecasts even when the demographics are slanted. That’s because, in theory, the incentives of the most active traders are financial rather than political. The idea is that they bet big when they’re sure of an outcome and bet small when they don’t really know what they’re talking about, regardless of what they’d personally rather happen. For example, one Polymarket user who put $55 on Bolsonaro commented, “I LOST MONEY BUT IM SO HAPPY I DID LETS GO LULAAAA.” Still, the reliability of these markets can depend on the amount of money sloshing around. Mansour denied that Kalshi’s Brazilian-market volatility problem had to do with a lack of trading volume, but volume really only picked up at the very end; as it did, the odds started to change. Something similar played out on Polymarket. As one Bloomberg columnist pointed out , when prediction markets beat the pollsters during the 2024 U.S. presidential election, trading volume on Polymarket was in the billions. This time, the platform saw about $250 million in all. Forecasting swings like those in Brazil and Wisconsin will almost certainly keep happening. The coming U.S. midterms will be a moment of increased visibility for an already visible industry—these probabilities are now baked into some live election coverage. And once exit polls are in, real-time markets might end up filling the information gap as everyone awaits the final tally. It may not really matter whether people understand the methodological differences between prediction markets and other forecasts, or whether people understand probabilities at all. Most Americans already oppose betting on elections. If Republicans somehow stage a comeback next week despite prediction markets’ forecasts of a blue wave—if these platforms seem to miss at all—these firms may end up losing the little credibility they’ve managed to build thus far. Possible Futures In every edition, I’ll share my thoughts on a few news stories I’m watching. The NBA announced a formal partnership with Kalshi and Polymarket on Monday, naming the firms its “preferred” prediction markets and giving them access to its data. The league also reached a memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agreeing to share information and cooperate with its regulations. The NHL already has a league-wide partnership with both firms, and UFC, the MLS, and the MLB have deals with Polymarket; after last year’s betting scandals , the NBA has had a somewhat-fraught relationship with gambling. Monday’s news suggests that the league is leaning in anyway. Front Office Sports reports that the NFL told Saquon Barkley, a running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, to divest his equity stake in Polymarket. Different leagues have different rules about whether players can invest in these platforms; the NBA, for example, allows up to 1 percent stakes . Kalshi is planning to launch prediction markets for the admission rates of top U.S. colleges. Among them: MIT, Johns Hopkins, Duke, the University of Chicago, and all of the Ivies. Why not? Kalshi invents random markets all the time. Here’s one about a law having to do with Californian goatherds. Both are part of an industry-wide effort to attach markets to much of modern life.

items.title: Créances en souffrance : la procédure, nerf de la guerre
items.description: Plus de 100 milliards de dirhams de créances en souffrance, soit 8,2 % des crédits à fin 2025 : derrière ce stock, le rapport de la rencontre nationale du 24 mars, tout juste mis en ligne, situe une bonne part du blocage dans la mécanique des procédures, de la création des garanties à la liquidation des entreprises. Il en tire une feuille de route en trois volets, adossée au nouveau Code de procédure civile. Organisée à Rabat par le ministère de la Justice et Bank Al-Maghrib, la rencontre est partie d’un constat que le wali, Abdellatif Jouahri, a formulé sans détour : ce stock bride le financement des entreprises, notamment des PME, et pèse sur la notation du secteur. La banque centrale agit déjà sur le versant prudentiel, avec une circulaire révisée en décembre 2025 qui crée la catégorie des créances sensibles, durcit les conditions de restructuration et élargit la définition du défaut. Elle travaille aussi sur l’encadrement d’un marché secondaire des créances et sur la dimension éthique du recouvrement amiable. Mais le recouvrement judiciaire relève du juge et de la procédure, d’où le groupe de travail mixte que le ministre Abdellatif Ouahbi a mis en avant avec la direction de la Supervision bancaire, ainsi que la plateforme numérique d’échange entre tribunaux et banques. Tout commence en amont, au moment où la garantie est constituée. Le notaire Mohamed Benjelloun Benkacem a rappelé que l’acte authentique confère aux conventions une force exécutoire immédiate et que le notaire, tenu à une obligation de résultat sur l’inscription des hypothèques, vérifie la situation du titre foncier, le rang de l’hypothèque et la régularité des décisions sociales qui autorisent les sûretés. Ce travail de sécurisation, soutenu par la lettre d’engagement qui permet de débloquer les fonds avant l’accomplissement des dernières formalités, conditionne ce que vaudra la garantie le jour où le débiteur défaille. Le premier verrou du contentieux se situe à l’entrée. Pour prononcer la déchéance du terme, l’article 109 de la loi 31.08 sur la protection du consommateur exige trois échéances impayées consécutives et une mise en demeure restée sans effet, dont la preuve de réception pèse sur la banque. À défaut, le juge n’accorde que les échéances échues et le dossier repart de zéro. Le magistrat Mubarak Boutalha a relevé qu’aucun texte ne fixe les mentions obligatoires de l’avertissement, ce qui conduit certaines juridictions à déclarer la demande irrecevable lorsque le montant de l’échéance, le taux ou les frais n’y figurent pas. D’autres rejettent les actions en restitution de meubles ou d’immeubles faute de tentative préalable de règlement amiable. Le représentant du Crédit du Maroc, Zied Fathi, a ajouté que, selon l’article 255 du Dahir des obligations et des contrats, le débiteur n’est en demeure qu’une fois mis en demeure, sauf clause contraire, que les intérêts de retard ne courent qu’à partir de cet acte, et qu’il n’interrompt la prescription que s’il est régulier et suivi d’une action en justice. Les banquiers y voient surtout une sanction disproportionnée. Pour Labib Zidane, d’Al Akhdar Bank, un vice dans la notification peut priver l’établissement de l’ensemble de ses droits, notamment lorsqu’il ne peut plus déclarer sa créance dans une procédure collective ou une saisie-arrêt, sans que la notion de délai raisonnable ne vienne tempérer la rigueur. Il a plaidé pour un arrêt unificateur de la Cour de cassation et pour une mise en cohérence du texte général et de la loi sur la protection du consommateur. L’avocat Abdellatif Omrani a décrit la face cachée de cette difficulté : adresses inexactes, débiteurs qui déménagent sans prévenir, sociétés domiciliées dans des sièges fictifs, refus de réception qui rouvre la porte aux exceptions de forme. Le Code de procédure civile de 2026 répond en autorisant, lorsque la notification est impossible ou l’adresse inconnue, le recours à celle figurant dans la base de la carte nationale d’identité électronique, et en ouvrant la voie à la notification par plateforme ou courriel. Un modèle unique de mise en demeure, fixé par arrêté, est également proposé. Vient ensuite l’étape la plus coûteuse en temps : la réalisation des garanties. Le magistrat Khaled Mimoun a énuméré les points de friction : des commissaires de justice jusqu’ici empêchés de conduire les ventes immobilières, une mise à prix parfois excessive, une publicité traditionnelle peu efficace, des actions en distraction ou en nullité du commandement utilisées pour gagner du temps, des pratiques divergentes d’un tribunal à l’autre. La réforme habilite les commissaires de justice à procéder aux ventes, plafonne à trois les séances d’adjudication et permet au juge de l’exécution de baisser la mise à prix de 10 à 30 %. Le président du tribunal contrôle désormais le sérieux des actions dilatoires par une ordonnance non susceptible de recours, et des amendes pouvant atteindre 10 000 dirhams sanctionnent les contestations abusives. La date de vente doit être fixée dans les quinze jours suivant l’expiration du délai d’opposition, avec un droit de surenchère de dix jours moyennant un dépôt supérieur d’un tiers au prix. M. Mimoun a aussi demandé de réécrire l’article 87 du Dahir sur l’immatriculation foncière pour lever l’ambiguïté sur le concours des inscriptions. Les établissements gardent la main sur plusieurs points de pratique. Selon Salaheddine Dak, du CIH Bank, de nouvelles inscriptions continuent d’être acceptées sur le titre foncier après le commandement immobilier, en contradiction avec ce même article 87, la ratification des ventes dépend parfois de l’appréciation du juge sans motivation suffisante, et la remise du produit de la vente aux créanciers tarde. Il a dénoncé en outre le refus de l’administration fiscale de distinguer vente amiable et vente judiciaire, qui entame la règle de purge. Pour les véhicules, Badreddine El Hafed, de la Sofac, a décrit une phase amiable de six à neuf mois avant tout recours au juge, au prix de véhicules restitués dégradés, parfois sans valeur marchande, tandis que les commissions rogatoires entre tribunaux alourdissent les frais. L’expertise judiciaire a nourri un débat à part. Le premier président de la Cour d’appel de commerce de Marrakech, Mohamed Sabir, a rappelé que l’expert éclaire le juge sans jamais le remplacer, et que certaines décisions l’ordonnent sans justifier sa nécessité. Il a pointé des difficultés techniques récurrentes : distinction entre compte courant et compte à vue, clôture du compte avant fixation du solde, écart entre taux conventionnel et taux appliqué, base de 365 ou de 366 jours, commissions sans fondement contractuel clair. Le magistrat Abdelouahed Moulada a souligné que le nouveau Code, dans ses articles 55 à 66, oblige le tribunal à vérifier la recevabilité de l’action avant toute mesure d’instruction et lui permet de renoncer à l’expertise lorsque l’affaire est en état. Du côté bancaire, Mohamed Ben Taleb, d’Attijariwafa bank, a dénoncé un recours devenu quasi automatique, même lorsque contrats et relevés sont limpides, l’absence de référentiel commun, qui produit des conclusions contradictoires, et un contrôle des experts plus administratif que technique. Parmi les remèdes évoqués figurent l’inscription de profils bancaires aux tableaux d’experts, des applications numériques uniformes et un outil unifié de calcul des intérêts. Le terrain le plus délicat reste celui des entreprises en difficulté. Le magistrat Hicham Mamar a présenté la procédure de sauvegarde, ouverte à la seule initiative du chef d’entreprise tant qu’il n’est pas en cessation de paiements, comme un outil préventif qui préserve la capacité de remboursement. Mustapha Aabdou, de Saham Bank, y a opposé la rigueur de la déchéance de la créance non déclarée dans les délais, y compris lorsqu’elle est non exigible ou imprécise, et la difficulté de déclarer des créances composées du principal, des intérêts et d’échéances futures. Il a réclamé une déclaration à titre conservatoire et des unités numériques dédiées. Le président du tribunal de commerce de Béni Mellal, Larbi Fares, a rappelé qu’une banque peut passer du statut de créancier à celui de débiteur si elle continue à financer une société dont elle connaît les difficultés, ou si elle suspend brutalement ses concours. Déclarer une créance garantie comme chirographaire fait en outre perdre les privilèges attachés. En liquidation, le créancier titulaire d’une sûreté peut reprendre les poursuites individuelles si le syndic n’a pas réalisé les actifs dans les trois mois. L’expert-comptable et syndic Fahd Mejbar a livré le chiffre le plus parlant : un taux de recouvrement de 5 à 30 %, et de 5 % seulement en liquidation judiciaire, contre environ 80 % aux États-Unis. Il a plaidé pour une préparation anticipée de la solution avant l’ouverture de la procédure, pour des plateformes permettant aux créanciers de suivre leurs dossiers, pour un régime simplifié destiné aux petites entreprises, et pour le respect du délai de quatre mois imparti au syndic pour rendre son rapport. Pour le crédit-bail, l’arrêt de la Cour de cassation du 3 avril 2025 confie au juge-commissaire la compétence exclusive pour constater la résiliation et ordonner la restitution tant que la procédure est ouverte, alors que les sociétés de financement relèvent à la fois du Code de commerce et de la loi bancaire, avec deux comptabilités parallèles, comme l’a regretté Abdallah Benhamida. La feuille de route distingue trois volets. Le premier regroupe cinq mesures à court terme : accompagnement du Code de procédure civile et du registre des procurations, généralisation de la plateforme « Tabadol », plateforme de vente aux enchères, outil de calcul des intérêts et notification électronique. Le deuxième renvoie à une concertation approfondie la révision du Livre V du Code de commerce, consacré aux difficultés de l’entreprise, que la proposition de procédure préparée à l’avance et le régime des petites entreprises viendraient compléter. Le troisième prévoit des ateliers techniques, une étude sur la médiation, un guide pratique et un observatoire national du recouvrement judiciaire. Les recommandations finales y ajoutent un plan d’action daté, un livre blanc, des formations nationales et régionales, une plateforme de la législation et de la jurisprudence bancaires, et un encouragement à la médiation et à l’arbitrage. Un comité de pilotage conjoint, assisté de trois comités techniques, supervisera l’exécution et remettra un rapport semestriel. Ses indicateurs porteront sur les délais moyens de jugement et d’exécution, les taux de recouvrement effectif, le volume des services numériques et le recours aux modes alternatifs, avec une révision annuelle des priorités et des échéances. The post Créances en souffrance : la procédure, nerf de la guerre appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026: les ambitions de l'équipe ivoirienne de basket 3x3 [4/5]
items.description: Parmi les sept disciplines où la Côte d’Ivoire est engagée aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) 2026, on dénombre le basket 3x3, une pratique urbaine devenue discipline olympique à part entière. La Côte d'Ivoire, qui connaît une reviviscence de ses sélections jeunes en basket, s'empare aussi du basket 3x3. Rencontre avec l'équipe ivoirienne du 3x3 à Abidjan, avant le départ de celle-ci à Dakar. L'occasion d'observer la préparation et les ambitions de cette équipe ivoirienne aux premiers JOJ en Afrique.

items.description: Australia has returned two stone sculptures to China after more than 30 years abroad. China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration received the heads on Wednesday, according to the state broadcaster CCTV. They are thought to have been removed from two imperial mausoleums in Henan...

items.description: Solo horas después de su llegada a Miami este miércoles tras huir de Brasil después de perder las elecciones frente a Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro hizo pública una carta dirigida al pueblo brasileño y a la comunidad internacional en la que afirmaba que su victoria le fue arrebatada mediante un “golpe de Estado” y se declaraba “el verdadero presidente” de su país. Sin embargo, esa carta ha tenido una vida corta: fue borrada y reemplazada por una nueva en la que el senador se autoproclama el “líder” de Brasil. La primera versión del texto, difundido en redes por políticos aliados, llevaba como membrete un escudo nacional que no se utiliza desde 1968. En la nueva versión, fue corregido. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Al menos 68 personas han muerto en un accidente ferroviario que se ha producido este miércoles por la mañana a la altura de la estación de Urda (Toledo). Un total de 53 heridos continúan siendo atendidos en hospitales de Castilla-La Mancha, mientras que 56 han recibido ya el alta. items.title: Le dialogue républicain ou le courage de se corriger: À propos du débat sur la loi de finances rectificative au Sénégal (Par Pr Khadiyatoulah Fall)
items.description: Les controverses autour du projet de loi de finances rectificative soulèvent une question qui dépasse le débat budgétaire : à quelles conditions un responsable peut-il reconnaître la pertinence d’un argument adverse sans perdre l’autorité nécessaire pour agir ? On appelle volontiers au dialogue. Mais on examine moins ce qui, dans nos façons de parler, de commenter et de soutenir les acteurs, peut le rendre impraticable. Lorsque toute concession devient une défaite, toute nuance une faiblesse et toute évolution un reniement, nous demandons aux responsables de se parler tout en leur interdisant de bouger. Nous installons ainsi une contradiction au cœur de la vie publique : nous souhaitons que la discussion améliore les décisions, mais nous sanctionnons ceux qui acceptent qu’elle modifie leur position. Ce mécanisme mérite attention. Un responsable ne s’adresse jamais seulement à son interlocuteur. Il parle devant ses partisans, ses adversaires et des citoyens qui interprètent ses gestes. Il peut reconnaître la force d’une objection et redouter le prix public de son acceptation. Dès lors, chacun défend aussi l’image de sa propre constance. La discussion avance dans les arguments, tandis que les positions restent figées dans les déclarations. Mettre le dialogue au cœur de la République, c’est rendre politiquement possible une correction publiquement justifiée. Une telle exigence engage les responsables, mais aussi leurs soutiens. Sommes-nous disposés à entendre celui que nous approuvons expliquer qu’un échange l’a conduit à revoir son jugement ? Lui reconnaissons-nous cette liberté lorsque nous avons applaudi sa fermeté ? La capacité de dialogue d’un acteur dépend aussi de la place que son propre camp laisse à son discernement. Toute évolution ne mérite cependant pas d’être saluée. Un engagement abandonné sans explication, un arrangement de convenance et une révision fondée sur des raisons sérieuses appellent des appréciations différentes. Celui qui modifie sa position doit pouvoir dire ce qu’il a appris, ce qu’il préserve, ce qu’il change et quelles conséquences il en attend. La correction devient alors un acte dont il répond devant les citoyens. Le débat budgétaire donne à cette exigence un contenu concret. Une prévision de recettes peut être trop optimiste. Une économie envisagée peut entraîner des dommages sociaux sous-estimés. Une dépense souhaitable peut reposer sur un financement incertain. Une objection parlementaire peut révéler une fragilité du projet ; une réponse gouvernementale peut faire apparaître une difficulté jusque-là insuffisamment considérée. La délibération prend son sens lorsque ces éléments peuvent effectivement transformer l’arbitrage. Le gouvernement doit donc expliciter les hypothèses et les conséquences de ses choix. Les parlementaires doivent préciser leurs objections et les modifications qu’ils souhaitent obtenir. Les citoyens doivent pouvoir comprendre ce que la discussion a permis de vérifier, de préserver ou de corriger. La qualité du dialogue se mesure à la possibilité réelle qu’un argument change quelque chose à la décision. La presse, les réseaux sociaux et les organisations citoyennes participent à cette possibilité. À force de demander qui a cédé, nous risquons de perdre de vue ce qui a été amélioré. Chaque concession transformée en humiliation rend la suivante plus difficile. Nos commentaires contribuent ainsi à ouvrir ou à fermer l’espace des solutions. Le désaccord républicain exige des convictions et leur mise à l’épreuve. Il laisse à chacun la responsabilité de défendre une position, tout en maintenant ouverte la possibilité de la réexaminer. Cette disponibilité doit accompagner le travail ordinaire des institutions, avant que les tensions ne rendent toute évolution suspecte. Le Sénégal gagnerait à faire de cette exigence une culture publique : demander des raisons à celui qui change, mais aussi à celui qui persiste malgré les objections. Nous aurons franchi un seuil démocratique lorsque l’autorité d’un responsable pourra grandir de la correction qu’il accepte d’expliquer. Par Khadiyatoulah Fall Professeur émérite

items.title: Liverpool overcome Chelsea in tense penalty shootout
items.description: Liverpool knocked out Chelsea on penalties to book their place in the Carabao Cup quarter-finals as Xabi Alonso and Jordan Henderson fell to a comeback on their return to Anfield. The tie inevitably went to a shootout after the teams finished level in normal time, with a Morgan Rogers penalty for the visitors cancelled out by a Cody Gakpo spot-kick at the other end. In a tense outcome, Valentin Barco hit the woodwork for Chelsea, but Kostas Tsimikas blazed over for Liverpool and former Reds captain Henderson levelled. Blues keeper Mike Penders then saved Ryan Gravenberch, but Giorgi Mamardashvili kept out Emmanuel Emegha’s effort; after Joe Gomez scored, French defender Wesley Fofana skied his spot-kick over. Liverpool secured their fifth straight penalty success against Chelsea as the 10-time winners booked an Anfield meeting with Andoni Iraola’s former club, Bournemouth. Both managers made several changes from the weekend’s Premier League games, with Iraola making seven after Liverpool’s win over Brighton. Alonso, who won the Champions League in 2005 as a player with the Reds, made four changes for Chelsea, with Henderson starting in the absence of suspended Cole Palmer and injured Joao Pedro. Neither goalkeeper had any saves to make in the opening stages, but the contest burst into life in the 40th minute when Gravenberch made a poor challenge on Moises Caicedo in the box, and referee Darren England awarded the Blues a penalty. Henderson picked up the ball and was met with a chorus of boos before handing to Rogers, who sent Mamardashvili the wrong way. But Chelsea’s joy was short-lived as Fofana handled the ball in the box just three minutes later. Cody Gakpo stepped up and sent Penders the wrong way for his 11th goal of the competition. Alonso had to make a change before half-time after centre-back Maxence Lacroix was injured and replaced by Levi Colwill. Just before the hour mark, Iraola turned to his bench and brought on Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola for Lewis Koumas and James McConnell, both booked in the first half. Liverpool upped the ante, and Chelsea remained a counter-attacking threat, but neither side could find a winner. Penders, who made an error in his side’s 2-0 home league loss to Spurs on Saturday, made two great saves to keep out Ronald Araujo and Barcola. At the other end, Marco Palestra forced Mamardashvili into a brilliant save, but surprisingly, Alonso didn’t bring Estevao on to try to make a difference. With no extra time, it went straight to penalties and could have gone either way until Fofana’s miss proved decisive. Analysis: Missed opportunity for Alonso as Reds extend winning run With Chelsea not in Europe and downbeat after their weekend loss to Tottenham, this competition represented a genuine opportunity for Alonso to win a major trophy and that was reflected by his team selection. His side didn’t make the best of starts at Anfield but once they took the lead, he will be disappointed their advantage lasted only three minutes. They still battled well and posed a threat, but the defeat will sting, particularly because they blew a golden opportunity to win the tie when Emegha had his effort saved. Much has been written about the friendship between Spaniards Alonso and Iraola, and while it is only three months into the new season, it’s clear Iraola has had the better start. He enters November having tasted defeat just once in all competitions. The mood around Anfield at full-time was jubilant, and Liverpool fans have now seen their team win their last five in a row, with the last three at home. Arsenal next on Sunday in the Premier League, and a test of where the Reds stand. Both Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot reached the final of this competition in their first season in charge, and Iraola will have his sights set on emulating them in the back of his mind.

items.title: ‘Two half-wounded people make a better whole’ : a couple’s journey of faith and advocacy for mental health
items.description: It’s hard to say who’s the more fascinating half of the Mardon marriage. In spite of their struggles with mental health and disability, Austin Mardon and his wife, Catherine, have a remarkable life, which is expressed most completely in the witness of their marriage. “Two half-wounded people make a better whole,” Austin Mardon told The B.C. Catholic, which recently interviewed the couple. The Mardons have dedicated their lives and their marriage to mental health advocacy and education. Some of their commitment has taken the form of writing, published in local Alberta publications, as well as The B.C. Catholic. Catherine Mardon is a lawyer and social justice advocate who was stabbed 17 times and left for dead in 1991 after testifying in court against a white supremacist group in the U.S. Midwest. She sustained a traumatic brain injury in the attack, but also left her assailant with broken teeth. She was one of the first lawyer in Oklahoma City to take on AIDS patients as clients, at a time when many firms wouldn’t. Over the decades, her advocacy has spanned issues from disability rights to access to justice, earning her recognition across North America, including the King Charles III Coronation Medal, the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond and Platinum Jubilee Medals, and, most recently, the Institute of International Peace Leaders, which honoured her with its Peace Award in March. Her husband, Dr. Austin Mardon, is a celebrated scientist and mental health advocate. Diagnosed with schizophrenia in early adulthood, he defied expectations by becoming a public figure and tireless advocate for those living with mental illness. While in his twenties, he suffered severe frostbite on a NASA-funded research expedition to Antarctica in 1986–87, where he became the first Canadian to discover a moon-origin meteorite. He is the founder of the Antarctic Institute of Canada, an organization dedicated to encouraging Canadian Antarctic research, and he holds numerous academic degrees and serves on several university and international science boards. In spring 2024, he was awarded an honorary doctor of laws degree from the University of British Columbia for his work on polar research, exploration, and environmental preservation, which included contributions to the academic and professional development of students at UBC. Austin Mardon in Antarctica during his research expedition in 1986. Austin’s Antarctic research camp at the Lewis Cliff-Beardmore Glacier Antarctica polar plateau. He is also a Member of the Order of Canada and a recipient of the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal and the King Charles III Coronation Medal. Despite their individual achievements, it’s their marriage that might be the most remarkable thing about them. The accomplishments of both Catherine and Austin are remarkable—and often shared. Together, they have opened their home to over a dozen children with Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS), legally adopting one of them. Many of these children arrived with significant behavioural and medical needs. Catherine first encountered FAS while still in college, when she took in her nephew who was born with the condition. His life was hard, and he later died at 24, following a struggle with addiction and prostitution. “Poor judgment and no impulse control,” she says. “Every FAS parent knows what that means.” So too did Pope Francis, and when the couple told the late Pontiff about their foster children, he lifted his hands to the sky and said, “I know!” The moment has stayed with them both. Still, they keep welcoming children. Asked why they took in so many, Catherine laughed: “It’s like potato chips. We’d always take another.” Individuals with FAS are notorious for disappearing, and often they struggle to show gratitude for kindness and concern. Still, the Mardons say they can always expect calls on Christmas or birthdays because their foster children know they are always remembered. There will always be a present in their stockings. The couple also co-author books for adults and children, often drawing from their work with the mentally ill and socially marginalized. Their children’s stories follow the adventures of a basset hound the couple once owned, named Gandy. The couple gave a copy of Gandy and the Man in White , a story about the dog’s visit to Rome, to Pope Francis during their 2019 audience. The books can be found at lulu.com. The couple now live in Edmonton, and their partnership is grounded in both faith and service. They are Knight and Dame Commanders in the Order of St. Sylvester—the highest papal honour a layperson can receive. Among other things, the title technically grants them permission to ride horseback through St. Peter’s Square and carry swords in the Pope’s presence, although Austin jokes that finding a horse big enough might prove tricky. The honours have come with more than ceremonial perks. When they met Pope Francis in 2017, they were ushered past security checks for a private papal audience. Catherine, who had lost much of her Spanish due to her brain injury, temporarily regained the ability to speak the language and held a brief conversation with the Holy Father—an experience she still describes as miraculous. Catherine Mardon playing her baritone trombone. Their Catholic faith is deeply interwoven with their life’s work, especially in the realm of mental health. Schizophrenia carries a 10 per cent suicide rate within the first decade of diagnosis, and 40 per cent of those living with the illness will attempt suicide at some point. Homelessness, substance abuse, and extreme social isolation are common. Managing the illness takes a strict regimen of shifting medications, personal resilience, and significant external support. The Mardons have chosen not only to face this challenge in their own home but to open their doors to others facing similar battles. Austin and Catherine Mardon at the dinner following Austin’s receiving the Order of Canada in 2007. There were skeptics early on. Because of their mental health conditions—Austin with his schizophrenia and Catherine managing the long-term effects of her traumatic brain injury—many doubted the couple’s intentions to marry. Austin’s family initially opposed the marriage, and for the first six months, Catherine says people frequently asked if she also had schizophrenia. But when Austin had the courage to tell her about his diagnosis, Catherine recognized in him something rare. While many with the illness retreat from society, Austin remained committed to his treatment and to life. The key, Catherine says, is separating the person from the illness. “When symptoms break through, you deal with the problem—not the person.” She also believes in commitment: “If you go in from the beginning without divorce as an option, you have to work through things.” As such, their relationship runs on communication and truth-telling. The pair complement each other well. Schizophrenia, which often affects a person’s ability to notice and understand social cues, sometimes works in Austin’s favour. He’s unflinching in situations that require difficult conversations or confrontation. His only complaint? “Catherine is too nice.” The result is a marriage built on faith, discipline, honesty, and a shared refusal to be defined by limitation.

items.title: Holders Man City urge past Brighton on penalties
items.description: Stand-in goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli was the hero, saving two penalties as holders Manchester City edged past Brighton in a shootout after a 2-2 draw to reach the Carabao Cup quarter-finals. Rulli kept out the final two spot kicks from Yasin Ayari and Lewis Dunk to send City through to face League One side Bradford City in the last eight. Brighton stunned the home crowd by going ahead on the half-hour mark through Malick Yalcouye’s close-range finish, converting Georginio Rutter’s cross. But five minutes before half-time, City drew level with a long-range strike from Mateo Kovacic that flew past Jason Steele and nestled in the bottom corner. Just seconds after the restart, Fabian Hurzeler’s side retook the lead following Rutter’s fine first-time finish from Jaouen Hadjam’s clever cutback. Brighton could have extended their lead further, but Rulli made a stunning fingertip save to deny Rutter a second, while the Frenchman also hit the side netting after going round the City goalkeeper. Rayan Cherki saw an effort deflect narrowly wide as City looked to claw their way back into the tie, before Vitor Reis flicked his low free-kick into the net with his outstretched foot. Substitute Mats Wieffer struck the post late in the second half for Brighton, but the match went to penalties before Rulli’s heroics sent City through.
