items.title: Catholic couple brings the love of family to young people with mental illness
items.description: For Catholic couple Austin and Catherine Mardon, mental illness is personal. Austin has schizophrenia, Catherine has PTSD, and together they foster children and young adults with Fetal Alcohol Syndrome. Austin and Catherine have been married since 2003. Both are writers, and their experiences have led them to devote themselves to working on behalf of people with mental illnesses, many of whom, they said, end up without a family and living on the street. The Mardons met Pope Francis after the general audience Nov. 6. They were inducted, in 2017, into the Pontifical Order of Pope Saint Sylvester, a papal Order of Knighthood, for their work on behalf of the disabled. A native of Oklahoma, Catherine told CNA she has always remembered what one of her childhood teachers, a Carmelite nun, once said: “We don’t help people because they’re Catholic, we help people because we’re Catholic and weʼre called to do it.” “Look around,” she said. There are people in need of love and support all around, but “don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid” to reach out. Austin, a Canadian, is an assistant adjunct professor of psychiatry at the University of Alberta. A scientist by education, Austin was part of a NASA meteorite recovery expedition to the Antarctic in the 1980s at the age of 24. Unfortunately, the extreme difficulties of the expedition affected him mentally and physically. Despite these challenges, he earned master’s degrees in science and education and published more articles and books, before being diagnosed at age 30 with schizophrenia, which he manages with medication. He has since also obtained a PhD in geography and continued to publish and speak extensively in the fields of science, mental illness and disability. Catherine was previously a lawyer focused on social justice issues, including death row appeals. She also helped the homeless and people with AIDs, and her work brought her into contact with many people struggling with mental illness. “I have helped people that most other ordinary people didn’t want to be in the same room with,” she said. After testifying in a case, Catherine was brutally attacked, leaving her with physical injuries, a traumatic brain injury, and PTSD. She was no longer able to practice law. But Austin and Catherine have taken their sufferings and transformed into an opportunity to help others. “When I got hurt and couldn’t practice law anymore, I didn’t just sit on a beach or curl up in a corner somewhere. I started taking care of people. Because that was something I could do, including [helping] a couple of kids who had Fetal Alcohol [Syndrome],” Catherine said. The difference between Fetal Alcohol Syndrome and other severe mental illnesses, like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, they said, is that there is no treatment, because it is caused by permanent brain damage before birth. The best thing for someone in this situation is early identification and intervention, Austin said, “to give them coping mechanisms to manage it, teach them techniques.” “It’s almost like teaching someone who is blind or deaf how to maneuver around a world that they can’t quite perceive,” he said. Catherine and Austin discovered, however, that many children and young adults with Fetal Alcohol Syndrome do not get early intervention. In many cases, due to poor family situations or a loss of their parents, they end up in foster care, and then, when they age out of the system, on the streets. So, the Mardons started taking some of these teenagers and young adults into their home. They also reach out to other young adults suffering from mental illness. They throw parties for them and invite them over for the holidays. “The most important thing when it comes to dealing with the disenfranchised is first you have to recognize their equal human dignity. And secondly, you have to take them where they are,” Catherine said. People automatically expect the mentally ill to be scary, she said. “They’re humans.” “They want to be invited to Sunday dinner… They want somebody to remember their birthday. They want somebody to invite them to Christmas.” The Mardons encourage others to find ways to support young people with mental illness, especially, they said, older adults who either do not have children or whose children are grown. Young adults leaving the foster care system are in need of the kind of support a family would offer, they said. While there are charities to provide financial support and resources, these individuals often miss out on the practical advice of a loved one and the chance to form healthy relationships with others. “Somebody’s got to take care of them,” Catherine said. Austin said what he would like Catholics – both priests and laity – to understand about mental illness is “that today there are effective treatments,” through both medication and therapy. He added that some Catholics think mental illness is a character flaw that can be solved by prayer. This is a dangerous misconception, he warned. “We don’t say that you should pray instead of take medication for your heart, but many Christians and Catholics believe that [mental illness] is a character flaw…It’s not a character flaw,” he emphasized. Austin often speaks on the topic, and he said his faith always informs his advice for people with mental illness or for their family members. “I think that faith without action can be very hollow,” he added, “but then action without faith can sometimes be misguided.

items.title: Liverpool beat Chelsea in League Cup shoot-out, Man City survive scare
items.description: Liverpool beat Chelsea in a dramatic penalty shoot-out to reach the League Cup quarter-finals, while holders Manchester City survived a scare against Brighton on Wednesday. In a clash between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso, it was the Liverpool manager who took the bragging rights in the last-16 tie at Anfield. A 1-1 draw in normal time set the stage for the shoot-out as Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers netted from the spot, only for Cody Gakpo to equalise with a penalty of his own just before half-time. Chelsea’s Valentin Barco hit the post in the shoot-out before Liverpool’s Kostas Tsimikas wasted a chance to win it when he blazed over. Ryan Gravenberch was denied by Chelsea keeper Mike Penders, but Giorgi Mamardashvili saved Emmanuel Emegha’s kick to keep Liverpool alive. After Joe Gomez scored for Liverpool, Blues defender Wesley Fofana miscued into the Kop as the hosts advanced. It was former Liverpool midfielder Alonso’s third defeat in his three visits to Anfield as a manager following losses with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid in 2025. In their debut campaigns at Liverpool, Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot both reached the League Cup final and Iraola is on course to follow in their footsteps with the 10-time winners of the competition. Alonso made just four changes to the Chelsea side that lost 2-0 at home to Tottenham on Saturday, while Iraola made seven changes from Liverpool’s 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday. Rogers put Chelsea in front with a 40th-minute penalty after Gravenberch clattered into Moises Caicedo. But Liverpool were level three minutes later with a penalty of their own as Gakpo converted from the spot following Fofana’s handball. At the Etihad Stadium, City were pushed to the brink by Brighton in a 2-2 draw before winning on penalties. City boss Enzo Maresca made nine changes after Saturday’s loss at Aston Villa — which ended the leaders’ 100 percent start to the Premier League campaign. – Rulli stars for City – Erling Haaland, Ruben Dias, Elliot Anderson and Gianluigi Donnarumma were among the City stars rested. Brighton went in front after 30 minutes when Malick Yalcouye steered Georginio Rutter’s shot past Geronimo Rulli from five yards. Mateo Kovacic hauled City level 20 minutes later with a fine finish that curled into the far corner from 25 yards. Rutter restored Brighton’s lead two minutes after half-time, slotting home from Jaouen Hadjam’s cut-back. Vitor Reis deflected in Rayan Cherki’s 72nd-minute free-kick to equalise for City. Kovacic’s penalty was saved by Jason Steele in the shoot-out, but Rulli denied Brighton’s Yasin Ayari and Lewis Dunk to send City into the last eight. The sides meet again in the Premier League at the Etihad on Saturday. Bournemouth extended their blistering run with a 3-0 win against Aston Villa at the Vitality Stadium. The Cherries beat AC Milan 3-0 in the Europa League last week and followed that up with a 3-0 win at Manchester United in the Premier League on Sunday. Marco Rose’s men dispatched Villa in equally emphatic fashion as goals from Amine Adli, Lewis Cook and Alvaro Rodriguez made it five successive wins in all competitions. Crystal Palace eased the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage with a 1-0 win at Fulham. Eddie Nketiah struck in the 37th minute to give struggling Palace their first win in five games in all competitions. Sunderland enjoyed a welcome respite from their Premier League struggles with a 3-2 victory against Brentford at the Stadium of Light. Sitting bottom of the Premier League, Sunderland swatted aside the Bees with goals from Chemsdine Talbi, Tymur Tutierov and Malick Fofana. Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago netted too late to save Brentford. Fourth-tier Fleetwood reached the quarter-finals with a stunning penalty shoot-out victory over Premier League champions Arsenal on Tuesday. Everton host Newcastle in the last game of the fourth round on Thursday. AFP The post Liverpool beat Chelsea in League Cup shoot-out, Man City survive scare appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Fast-changing world leaves youth little time for the apprenticeship I had – Kufuor
items.description: Former President John Agyekum Kufuor says today’s youth may not have time for the long apprenticeship that prepared him for leadership. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said rapid technological change demands a quicker transfer of experience between generations. “I say I came to what I eventually ended in through long apprenticeship. They may not be privileged to undergo such an apprenticeship with time.” Kufuor traced his development through legal studies, law practice and city administration. The world moved more slowly then, allowing him to learn through successive roles. Today’s young people face a different pace, driven by new technologies, including artificial intelligence. He said that shift places a responsibility on older generations. They must turn their accumulated experience into lessons young people can absorb and apply quickly. “So my generation should feel a responsibility to sort of package the experiences we had to go through to get to where we are, because I believe in the intergenerational evolution of society.” He explained that this responsibility is part of his motivation to leave a legacy through his foundation. The John A. Kufuor Foundation promotes effective leadership, good governance and socioeconomic development. Its Kufuor Scholars Program offers university students three years of leadership preparation through mentorship, coaching, skills training and practical activities. The programme seeks to nurture patriotic, selfless and community-minded leaders. It also encourages creative thinking and ethical problem-solving to prepare young people to contribute to national development. For Kufuor, this support should build on the strengths young people already possess. “I tend to believe the current generation is far better educated than our generation.” He pointed to their preparation in science and technology, as well as their access to information through mobile phones. Recalling Kumasi in the 1950s and 1960s, he contrasted the limited availability of telephones with the tools now within young people’s reach. He said those tools let them learn quickly. His generation’s task is to make its experience accessible enough to help them advance. He expects that combination of modern education and inherited experience to give young people insights into how earlier generations developed society—and equip them to do better.

items.title: How Elon Musk Turned on Ukraine
items.description: O n October 11 , a confidential memo went out to military officers across Ukraine, urging them to brace for a catastrophe. Donald Trump had decided earlier that week to ease U.S. sanctions on Russia and to begin buying its diesel fuel. Based on that shift in White House policy, the memo foresaw another act of American betrayal: the loss of access to the Starlink satellite network, which Ukraine uses to operate its drone fleet. The document warned that Elon Musk, the creator of Starlink, might soon restrict service in Ukraine, and it urged users of the technology to “keep all communication alternatives to Starlink on standby—ready for immediate use—and develop contingency plans.” Two days later, the warnings began to come true. Starlink faltered across the war zone, grounding drones and halting military operations. In one case, it led to the loss of Ukrainian naval drones in the Black Sea, according to two people familiar with that mission. The memo predicted worse to come. It came from a nongovernmental organization called Narodnyi Starlink, or “People’s Starlink,” which helps the armed forces of Ukraine acquire and operate this technology. In the memo, the group’s founder, Volodymyr Stepanets, envisioned several ways Musk could restrict service. The worst-case scenario—a total shutoff—would result in a cascade of disasters, potentially leading to Russia’s victory in the war. One senior U.S. military officer told us that “without Starlink, the war would grind to a halt.” Musk himself has suggested that might be his goal. In a series of posts on X over the weekend, he admitted to causing last week’s outages, and he lashed out at those who call for greater military aid to Ukraine. “I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict,” Musk wrote. “May you burn in hell.” Since the disruption, Ukraine and its allies have scrambled to find a replacement for Starlink, which relies on the world’s largest constellation of satellites to deliver high-speed-internet access anywhere in the world. But nothing comparable exists. The most promising effort in Ukraine to build such a system faced a major setback this summer, when its architect, Dmytro Stetsenko, died of apparent heart failure at the age of 46. European attempts to replicate Starlink are years away from matching its scale, and most of these efforts depend on Musk’s aerospace company, SpaceX, to launch their satellites into orbit. Russia, by contrast, has its own fleet of space rockets, and it is racing to field a network of satellites that can rival Starlink. The system, known as Rassvet, or “Sunrise,” would give Russia an “asymmetric advantage” in the war, says Andrey Liscovich, a co-founder of the Ukraine Defense Fund, which has helped secure thousands of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military. “They will be precise enough to fly these low-cost, jet-powered drones through a window anywhere in Ukraine,” Liscovich told us. Without Starlink, Ukraine would not be able to respond. Vladimir Putin said today that Russia has stayed in touch with Musk about Starlink. “Elon Musk is a genius, really a genius,” the Russian leader said at a televised summit in Moscow. He praised SpaceX for taking the lead in the race to develop this technology. “We are only taking the first steps,” Putin said of Russia’s answer to Starlink. “We are in close touch with our American colleagues, including Mr. Musk, because in orbit it is very important not to get in each other’s way.” This account of Musk’s turn against Ukraine is based on interviews with more than a dozen U.S. and Ukrainian officials, military officers, drone manufacturers, and experts on Starlink. Most of them spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive military operations and private negotiations. Several of them have dealt with Musk and his company directly since the start of the war, in 2022, and they have seen his views on Ukraine shift from generous support to outright hostility. If anything can yet restrain Musk from abandoning Ukraine, it may be his own financial interests. His company has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from the Starlink terminals operating in the war zone. Liscovich estimates there are well over 250,000 of them. In the past, SpaceX, which runs Starlink, has reportedly charged the Ukrainian government $2,500 per terminal each month, and it has cut off service when bills go unpaid. Earlier this month, when U.S. military officials asked SpaceX about the outages in Ukraine, the company advised switching to an upgraded contract to restore Ukraine’s access, U.S. officials told us. (Musk and SpaceX did not respond to questions for this article.) In June, SpaceX held the biggest initial public offering in history, earning a valuation of roughly $1.8 trillion. Revenue from Starlink keeps SpaceX investors happy and bankrolls Musk’s other projects, including his obsession with colonizing Mars. If he pulls the plug on Starlink in Ukraine, other countries could deem the service unreliable and accelerate the race to build an alternative. But those projects will not be ready until next year at the earliest. Until then, the world’s richest man will be largely free to decide Ukraine’s fate. [ From the November 2026 issue: Choose your overlord ] W hen the war began , Musk seemed eager to help Ukraine defend itself. Russia used missile strikes and cyber weapons to take down Ukraine’s digital infrastructure in the opening days of the invasion. To keep the country online, Musk donated thousands of Starlink antennas to its hospitals, power plants, government ministries, and various humanitarian causes. Soon, the Ukrainian military began using the service to pilot its drones and stay connected in the war zone. The service provided a critical advantage: The Russians had no access to Starlink and no way to jam its signal, which allowed Ukraine’s drones to crisscross the battlefield, dropping bombs on Russian troops. Images of these attacks spread online in 2022, and they caused alarm at SpaceX headquarters in Texas. “More and more people became uncomfortable,” a former SpaceX engineer who worked on the system’s development told us. Some of his colleagues left the company in protest. Their team had designed Starlink to give people internet access in places where broadband cannot reach, like hiking trails and ships at sea, not to wage a war. Musk also had apprehensions. In September 2022, Ukrainian officials asked him to switch on Starlink in the Black Sea. They wanted to use it in a sneak attack against Russian warships near the occupied region of Crimea. Musk refused. “Starlink was not meant to be involved in wars,” he said around that time to his biographer, Walter Isaacson. “It was so people can watch Netflix and chill and get online for school and do good peaceful things, not drone strikes.” At the end of 2022, Musk announced the launch of a service called Starshield. Reserved for military clients, it costs far more to use than Starlink. In Ukraine’s case, the U.S. government has paid for a lot of that service, handing Musk’s company a sizable windfall. In exchange, the Pentagon gets more control over Ukraine’s access to the satellites. Colin Kahl, then the U.S. undersecretary of defense, negotiated this arrangement with SpaceX, and he later told The New Yorker that it would “prevent Musk from turning off the switch.” But, for the most part, the Ukrainian military did not transition to using Starshield. It continued to use regular Starlink antennas, the kind available at Walmart and other retailers around the world. Their service costs as little as $30 a month, compared to as much as $25,000 for Starshield. The fine print in the Starlink user agreement bans its use for military purposes. But Musk’s company did not enforce that rule in Ukraine. It maintained the pretense that Starlink would be reserved for peaceful purposes, while the military would rely on Starshield antennas, largely paid for by American taxpayers. The reality was quite different. “They’re using it for everything,” the senior U.S. military officer told us of Ukrainian reliance on Starlink. “Drones, command and control, tactical communication on the battlefield.” The U.S. government has not disclosed how many Starshield terminals it has provided to Ukraine. But Ukrainian officials and experts told us that they account for less than one percent of all the terminals in the war zone. The rest are regular Starlinks purchased on the retail market, including thousands bought in bulk for Ukraine by the governments of Poland and Germany. “Officially, these were supposed to be for humanitarian use,” a person who has negotiated with SpaceX on Ukraine’s behalf told us. “But everybody knew that they are going to the military.” T his wink-wink arrangement put Ukraine in a dangerous spot. To operate its drone fleet and stay online in the war zone, its armed forces had no choice but to break the rules of Starlink service. “It’s much cheaper that way, and easier to scale,” a Ukrainian official told us. The military could get as many Starlink terminals as it needed through foreign donors and the commercial market. It could attach them to drones and launch them at the Russians without thinking twice about the cost. Starshield, by contrast, is far more expensive and only available in small batches through official government channels. This spring, the U.S. military faced a similar dilemma in the Middle East. According to a Reuters report that cited Pentagon documents, U.S. forces used Starshield to pilot their drones for strikes against Iran. When SpaceX found out, it raised the price for Starshield service in that region from roughly $5,000 per terminal per month to $25,000. The Pentagon agreed to pay. In Ukraine, Musk could be attempting a similar upsell. By enforcing the ban on military use of Starlink, he could oblige the Ukrainian military and its foreign allies to pay much more for Starshield. Musk’s explanation for the outages this month suggest he would be fine with that approach, even though it could allow the war to continue. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” he wrote on X on Saturday. “That loophole was closed last week.” The statement confused a lot of Starlink clients in Ukraine. For military users, the loophole still appears to be open and the service operational. Ukraine’s defense minister announced at the end of last week that Starlink service had returned to normal in the war zone. Two military officers told us that drones equipped with Starlink terminals have resumed their flights, including strikes on Russian forces. They realize, of course, that Musk could ground them again whenever he wants, and the next outage could last much longer—as the memo from People’s Starlink forewarned. “We have one very serious weak spot, and that’s our dependence on Starlink,” Denys Shtilerman, one of Ukraine’s most prolific drone developers, told us. “Next year we’ll address it,” he said. “Before that, America will have enormous leverage, the ability to blackmail us.” Developing a Starlink alternative could take much longer than a year, and it would be unlikely to succeed without Musk’s help. Roughly 90 percent of all the mass delivered into orbit travels on SpaceX rockets. Even Europe’s main competitor to Starlink, a French-British project known as the OneWeb network, relies on SpaceX to launch its satellites. Last month, the parent company of OneWeb announced plans to spend a billion euros to procure 229 additional satellites by 2034. That would bring its total to around 1,000—a fraction the size of the Starlink network, which includes more than 11,000 satellites, the largest constellation by far. [ Read: The new subterranean front ] With the recent disruptions in Ukraine, Musk showed that he can cut off the service any time he wants. The memo from People’s Starlink described the several ways he has to do that. Stepanets, its author, noted that Musk could start charging more for the use of Starshield antennas, forcing the U.S. government to pay up or cancel the service. In the most extreme case, the company could block Ukraine’s access entirely. Musk’s statements appear to countenance that. But Stepanets noted that such a move could blow up in Musk’s face. “Radical blackouts and humanitarian catastrophes make for a very bad public image,” he wrote in the memo. They would also not do much to help SpaceX’s profit margins or its stock price. Such considerations could restrain Musk’s urge to abandon Ukraine. But, either way, it will be his choice to make. Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer contributed reporting.

items.title: Ballon d’Or winner Kane watches as Bayern cruise into German Cup last 16
items.description: Newly-crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane was left on the bench as Bayern Munich sailed to a 6-1 win over second-tier Magdeburg in the German Cup last 32 on Wednesday. Bayern had no difficulty without their star striker, with Michael Olise grabbing a double and Ismael Saibari, Alphonso Davies, Nathaniel Brown and teenager David Santos Daiber also getting on the scoresheet. Kane received a guard of honour from his Bayern teammates before kick-off as the 75,000 fans at the Allianz Arena saluted the Ballon d’Or winner, two days after his triumph in London. Bayern got some more good news pre-match, with coach Vincent Kompany discharged from hospital, five days after collapsing at training on Friday. “We’re also winning for him of course,” Brown said of Kompany. “It’s really good that he’s back home now. He should get some rest, but hopefully we’ll see him again soon.” Olise tapped in an excellent Saibari assist from close range after 10 minutes but the unfancied visitors levelled five minutes later through Mateusz Zukowski. Olise returned the favour by setting up Saibari midway through the opening half and added a third from the spot early in the second half before smiling and pointing to Kane, Bayern’s regular penalty taker, on the bench. Teenage forward Lennart Karl set up goals for Davies and Brown before Santos Daiber added more gloss to the victory with a stoppage-time goal. Kane remained on the bench for the entire match, with Saturday’s home Bundesliga clash with Borussia Dortmund in mind. Bayer Leverkusen came from two goals down to win 5-2 against Nuremberg, with defender Edmond Tapsoba netting twice and Patrik Schick, Jonas Hofmann and Lucas Vazquez scoring goals. Earlier on Wednesday, Germany forward Deniz Undav’s 90th-minute strike took Stuttgart to a 1-0 win at 10-man Paderborn. Stuttgart, finalists in 2025, had a one-man advantage after Laurin Curda’s 37th-minute red card but could not break down a stubborn Paderborn. After striker Ermedin Demirovic had two efforts saved, Undav took matters into his own hands and turned in a Chris Fuehrich cross with extra time looming. “The win is what matters most,” Undav said. “I honestly don’t care whether I’m the one who scores, and that’s the truth. We won, we’re through to the next round — on we go.” Japan forward Keisuke Goto scored twice in the final 15 minutes to overturn a 2-1 deficit as Freiburg won 3-2 at home against Wolfsburg. Goto’s Japan teammate Kento Shiogai also bagged a brace, while Freiburg’s Igor Matanovic opened the scoring. Elsewhere, second-division sides Dynamo Dresden and Hertha Berlin both won 2-0 against Schalke and Jeddeloh respectively, while Kaiserslautern eliminated Hannover. items.title: Meteorites: Nature’s free sample return
items.description: Long before spacecraft visited the Moon, landed on asteroids, or returned samples from distant worlds, scientists were already studying material from beyond Earth. These extraterrestrial rocks, meteorites have often been described as the “poor man’s space probe” because they provide direct physical evidence from space without the expense and technological complexity of launching a spacecraft. Missions such as Apollo, Hayabusa2, and OSIRIS-REx have transformed our understanding of the Solar System. Yet meteorites remain among the most valuable scientific resources available for studying its origin, evolution, and composition. They preserve evidence from the earliest stages of planetary formation, record geological processes that occurred billions of years ago, and provide information that continues to guide modern planetary exploration. The sample return capsule from NASAs OSIRIS REx mission is seen shortly after touching down in the desert Sunday Sept 24 2023 at the Department of Defenses Utah Test and Training Range Image Credit NASAKeegan Barber Natural Messengers from Space Meteorites are fragments of extraterrestrial material that survive passage through Earth’s atmosphere and reach the ground. Most originate from asteroids, particularly those in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, where collisions eject rocky fragments into independent orbits around the Sun. Over millions of years, gravitational interactions gradually alter those orbits until some intersect Earth’s path. As these objects enter Earth’s atmosphere at high velocity, they compress and heat the surrounding air, producing the luminous phenomenon known as a meteor, or “shooting star.” Material that survives atmospheric entry and reaches the ground is called a meteorite. A meteor captured during the height of the Perseid shower in August 2018 in Cedar Breaks National Monument Utah Image Credit NASABill Dunford While most meteorites come from asteroids, a small number originate from the Moon or Mars. Powerful impacts can eject surface rocks into space, where they may travel for millions of years before eventually reaching Earth. Other meteorites preserve fragments of ancient planetary bodies that were disrupted by collisions during the Solar System’s early history. Unlike telescopes, which study distant objects through reflected or emitted light, meteorites allow researchers to conduct direct laboratory analyses. Scientists can measure chemical compositions, isotopic abundances, mineral structures, magnetic properties, and microscopic organic compounds. In many cases, these investigations provide information that cannot be obtained through remote observations alone. Robotic missions investigate carefully selected destinations and provide the geological context surrounding their samples. Meteorites, by contrast, arrive from a broad range of parent bodies, sometimes revealing unexpected minerals, chemical signatures, or geological processes that later become priorities for dedicated exploration missions. Time Capsules from the Birth of the Solar System Meteorites are generally classified into three major categories: stony meteorites, iron meteorites, and stony-iron meteorites. Stony meteorites account for approximately 94 percent of observed falls and consist primarily of silicate minerals. Among them, chondrites are particularly important because they contain tiny spherical structures called chondrules that formed during the earliest stages of Solar System development. Many chondrites have remained relatively unchanged for more than 4.5 billion years, preserving evidence of the materials from which the planets formed. Chondrite meteorite showing internal structure including chondrules metal grains matrix fusion crust and calcium rich inclusions diagram hand drawn schematic vector Image Credit Shutterstock Alexander P Achondrites originated from bodies that underwent melting and differentiation, producing rocks resembling terrestrial igneous formations. Iron meteorites consist primarily of iron-nickel alloys and generally represent material from the metallic cores of differentiated asteroids. Stony-iron meteorites contain mixtures of silicate minerals and iron-nickel metal. Some may preserve material from deep within differentiated asteroids, while others record the mixing of rocky and metallic material during major impacts. One of the greatest contributions of meteorite research has been determining the age of the Solar System. Radiometric dating of calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (CAIs) found in primitive meteorites places the formation of the earliest Solar System solids at approximately 4.567 billion years ago. These measurements provide the basis for establishing the age of the Solar System. These inclusions formed at extremely high temperatures near the young Sun, before the planets had fully developed. Primitive chondrites also contain presolar grains—microscopic mineral fragments that originated in stars that existed before our Sun. Their unusual isotopic signatures identify them as material formed outside the Solar System and subsequently incorporated into the building blocks of planets. Meteorites also preserve evidence of planetary differentiation. As early planetesimals grew, heat generated partly by radioactive decay caused some to melt. Dense metals such as iron and nickel sank toward their centers, while lighter silicate materials formed mantles and crusts. Collisions subsequently exposed and dispersed fragments of these internal structures. Iron meteorites can therefore provide samples of ancient planetary cores, while different classes of stony meteorites preserve evidence of crustal and mantle processes. These samples allow scientists to study stages of planetary development that would otherwise remain inaccessible. Clues to the Evolution of Other Worlds Meteorites record what happened as planets and smaller bodies formed, changed, collided, and sometimes broke apart. By comparing the elemental and isotopic compositions of different meteorite classes, scientists can investigate how materials were distributed throughout the early Solar System. Bodies that formed closer to the Sun generally contain fewer volatile materials, while some meteorites associated with more distant regions contain greater amounts of water-bearing minerals and organic compounds. Subsequent heating, collisions, and planetary migration have also influenced these distributions. Meteorites preserve records of ancient magnetic fields. Iron-bearing minerals can retain evidence of the magnetic environment in which they cooled. Paleomagnetic studies suggest that some asteroids once possessed molten metallic cores capable of generating magnetic dynamos similar in principle to Earth’s. These findings indicate that even relatively small planetary bodies could have experienced substantial internal geological activity. The violent history of the Solar System is recorded in meteorites as well. High-pressure minerals, deformation patterns, and melt veins preserve evidence of powerful collisions. By studying these features, scientists can better understand impact processes and interpret craters observed across the Moon, Mars, Mercury, and numerous asteroids. Water, Organics, and the Ingredients for Life Among the most intriguing discoveries from meteorite research is evidence that water and organic compounds were widespread in the early Solar System. Carbonaceous chondrites contain hydrated minerals that formed through interactions with liquid water on their parent asteroids. They also contain amino acids, nucleobases, and numerous complex organic compounds. In many cases, isotopic measurements demonstrate that these materials originated beyond Earth rather than resulting from contamination after the meteorites landed. These discoveries do not prove that life originated in space. They do demonstrate that some of the chemical ingredients associated with life existed beyond Earth and were present during the period when our planet was forming. During its early history, Earth experienced repeated impacts from asteroids and comets. Such objects may have delivered water, carbon compounds, phosphorus-bearing minerals, and other substances important to prebiotic chemistry. Although the origin of life remains an active area of research, meteorites provide evidence that some of its fundamental chemical building blocks were not unique to Earth. This connection has made meteorite research an important part of astrobiology. Understanding where water and organic materials formed, how they were distributed, and whether they survived planetary formation helps scientists evaluate environments elsewhere in the Solar System where conditions suitable for life may once have existed. The presence of water-bearing minerals also interests researchers studying asteroid resources. Water and other volatile materials could eventually support human activity beyond Earth, including life-support systems and the production of spacecraft propellants. Pieces of the Moon and Mars A small percentage of meteorites originate from the Moon and Mars. Lunar meteorites form when powerful impacts eject material from the Moon’s surface into space. Some fragments eventually reach Earth, providing samples that complement those returned by Apollo astronauts. Because lunar meteorites can originate from regions never visited by spacecraft, they expand our understanding of the Moon’s geological diversity. Martian meteorites have made an equally important contribution. Large impacts on Mars can accelerate surface rocks beyond the planet’s escape velocity. After traveling through space, a small number eventually intersect Earth’s orbit and survive passage through our atmosphere. Their Martian origin is supported by mineralogical and chemical analyses, including gases trapped in certain specimens whose composition matches measurements of the Martian atmosphere obtained by the Viking landers. These meteorites have allowed scientists to examine Martian material in terrestrial laboratories without waiting for spacecraft to return samples from the planet. Analyses reveal evidence of volcanic activity, water-rock interactions, and changes in the Martian environment over billions of years. They also help researchers interpret observations made by modern rovers and orbiters. However, an important limitation remains: scientists generally cannot determine the precise geological locations from which these meteorites originated. Sample-return missions address this limitation by collecting material from documented locations. Meteorites provide samples that nature delivers to Earth; spacecraft allow researchers to select where to explore and what material to collect. Meteorites and Modern Space Exploration Despite their scientific value, meteorites have limitations. Their arrival on Earth is uncontrolled, and atmospheric entry favors materials capable of surviving intense heating and mechanical stresses. Weathering after landing can alter their original chemistry and mineralogy, while the absence of geological context makes some observations difficult to interpret. Dedicated spacecraft missions provide information that meteorites cannot. They can examine surface features, map geological formations, measure local environmental conditions, and collect samples from carefully selected locations. Modern analytical techniques continue to increase the value of meteorite collections. Electron microscopy reveals nanoscale structures, mass spectrometry measures isotopic compositions with extraordinary precision, and X-ray imaging allows scientists to examine internal features without destroying specimens. Rocks collected decades or even centuries ago can yield new information as laboratory capabilities improve. A scientist holds up a vial that contains part of the sample from asteroid Bennu delivered to Earth by NASAs OSIRIS Rex Image Credit James Tralie Meteorites also have a role in preparing for future exploration. Their chemical and mineralogical compositions help researchers understand the diversity of asteroids and evaluate the materials that may be available on these bodies. Water, metals, and other resources found in asteroids could eventually support propellant production, construction, and life-support systems. Understanding the nature and distribution of these materials is an important consideration in developing technologies for using resources found beyond Earth, a process known as in-situ resource utilization. Meteorite research alone cannot establish whether a particular asteroid contains economically or technically accessible resources. That requires detailed observations and, in many cases, direct exploration. Nevertheless, laboratory studies provide essential information about the materials spacecraft may encounter. Spacecraft observations also help scientists interpret meteorite samples. Both approaches will remain important as exploration extends to more distant destinations. Connecting People with Space Meteorites play an important educational and cultural role. Museums and educational institutions display specimens that visitors can examine and, in some cases, touch. For students, holding a meteorite provides a direct physical connection to material that originated beyond Earth. Collections recovered from deserts and Antarctica continue to expand opportunities for scientific research. Antarctic ice fields are particularly valuable because glacial movement can concentrate meteorites in areas where their dark surfaces make them relatively easy to identify against the ice. In the 1986 87 expedition to Antarctica significant meteorite discoveries were made as part of the United States Antarctic Program USAP focused on the Beardmore Glacier area particularly the Lewis Cliff and Ice Tongue regions During this expedition over 700 meteorites were recovered Image Credit Dr Austin Mardon These collections support research, education, and public engagement. They also demonstrate that important discoveries about the Solar System do not always require traveling into space. Looking to the Future Meteorites have played an important role in advancing our understanding of the Solar System. They have helped establish its age, revealed the internal structures of ancient planetary bodies, documented the chemistry of planetary formation, and provided direct samples from the Moon and Mars. Their scientific value has not diminished with the development of increasingly sophisticated spacecraft. Laboratory studies of meteorites continue to complement robotic exploration and sample-return missions, particularly in understanding planetary composition, geological processes, and the distribution of water and other materials. As humanity expands its exploration of the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, this knowledge will become increasingly important. Understanding the composition and history of these bodies can help guide future missions and inform efforts to identify and utilize resources beyond Earth. “Nature’s Free Sample Return” remains an indispensable scientific resource. These natural samples have helped scientists reconstruct the Solar System’s past and will continue to contribute to its exploration. By Dr. John Christy Johnson, Dr. Peter Anto Johnson, Dr. Austin Mardon, and Burt Dicht

items.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
items.description: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said. The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36. Citing the medical examiner’s report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had “concluded its investigation” into her death. The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment. “Based on the Medical Examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental,” police said in a statement. Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere’s death, according to the BBC’s US media partner CBS News. A spokesperson for Greenville Police Department could not comment on what the DEA was investigating when contacted by the BBC. Panettiere, who had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse , was found unresponsive in a South Carolina residence on 16 August. Last month, the Greenville County Coroner’s Office confirmed the former child star had died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl – a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone. The coroner also found methocarbamol – a prescription muscle relaxant – and quetiapine – an anti-psychotic medication used to treat certain mental health conditions. The coroner’s office had said crews treated a woman in “cardiac arrest” and her autopsy showed “no signs of trauma” contributing to her death. Panettiere’s ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson – who has admitted to abusing her – and his brother Zack were with her when emergency services arrived, according to a police report from the day she died.

items.title: Laprophan obtient le visa de l'AMMC pour son introduction en bourse
items.description: Le groupe Laprophan a obtenu, mercredi, le visa de l'Autorité marocaine du marché des capitaux (AMMC) pour son introduction à la Bourse de Casablanca. Cette introduction en bourse, d’un montant global maximum de 2.222.535.700 dirhams, a pour ambition d’accompagner son développement actuel et de soutenir la croissance externe, dont la nouvelle acquisition en cours, ainsi que de renforcer la structure financière du Groupe et d’accompagner son développement industriel, indique un communiqué de Laprophan. Elle sera réalisée par voie d’augmentation du capital social réservée au public à hauteur d’un montant (prime d’émission incluse) de 1.399.975.500 dirhams, et de cession au public de 2.412.200 actions existantes détenues par MC IV Pharma et MC IV Morocco pour un montant maximal de 822.560.200 dirhams. À l’issue de l’Opération, les actions offertes au public représenteront 37,64% du capital et des droits de vote. La période de souscription est prévue du 9 au 17 novembre 2026 inclus. Le prix de l’action est fixé à 341 dirhams. Les actions du groupe Laprophan seront en vente dans toutes les agences bancaires et sociétés de bourse membres du syndicat de placement. CFG Finance est le Conseiller financier et coordinateur global de l’Opération. Pionnier national et acteur de référence multinational, le groupe Laprophan a pour vocation de mettre à la disposition des professionnels de santé et des patients des médicaments et solutions thérapeutiques de qualité, au service de la santé publique, de l'efficience des soins et de la souveraineté sanitaire. Fort d'une histoire de plus de 75 ans, initiée en 1949 par le Dr Abderrahim Bennis, Laprophan s'impose aujourd'hui comme une plateforme pharmaceutique multinationale intégrée de référence. Présent sur l'ensemble de la chaîne de valeur du médicament — de la recherche et développement (R&D) à la commercialisation, en passant par la fabrication et la distribution —, le groupe Laprophan s'appuie sur un modèle intégré multi-pôles. The post Laprophan obtient le visa de l'AMMC pour son introduction en bourse appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Corruption Catches Up to MAGA
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. One fundamental truth of politics is that ultimately all voter decisions come down to money. That’s why Dwight Eisenhower blew out Adlai Stevenson in 1956; it’s what James Carville meant when he declared, “It’s the economy, stupid,” in 1992; and it’s the reason that Joe Biden tried in vain to convince Americans that they were doing better than they believed during his presidency. This was also why some Democratic politicians and strategists counseled candidates not to place Donald Trump and his scandals at the center of their campaign. Better to focus on “kitchen table” issues, such as inflation and housing costs, they argued. To a great extent, this seems to have worked. Economic worries have been a consistent theme throughout the midterms, and Democrats appear poised to fare well. They’ve been helped by Trump, who has not only dismissed worries about affordability as a “hoax,” but has also gone out of his way to worsen inflation by launching a war in Iran. I wrote just last week that the economy explained GOP struggles. Yet an interesting thing has popped up in opinion surveys over the past couple weeks. A Fox News poll finds that corruption is the top issue for voters, edging inflation, gas prices, and health care. CNBC gets the same result : “Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey.” The Financial Times has similar findings: “About 69 per cent of registered voters, and almost 50 per cent of those who voted for the president in 2024, said they were ‘very’ or ‘somewhat’ concerned about ‘corruption, self-dealing or conflicts of interest’ in the Trump administration.” The idea that the economy alone explained Trump’s unpopularity was never entirely convincing. He has almost always had poor approval ratings, even when presiding over a strong economy. He didn’t win the popular vote in 2016; House Republicans were shellacked in 2018, when he made the election about him; he lost in 2020; and the GOP underperformed in 2022, under his influence. He was able to win only in 2024, when the elections centered on voters’ views of the Biden presidency. One big reason for these repeated voter rejections is the miasma of scandal that follows Trump wherever he goes. “When elections are clearly about Trump and MAGA, MAGA will lose,” Michael Podhorzer, a progressive strategist, told me in 2022 . Still, this finding is reassuring about voters’ discernment. My colleague Anne Applebaum has been foremost among many observers who have deemed this the most corrupt presidency in U.S. history. Even as the president and his family have made billions from his office, no single story seems to have broken through: no Teapot Dome, no Watergate, not even a Whitewater. The new polls on corruption, combined with Trump’s steadily declining favorability , suggest that rather than any single news story producing an inflection point—like the swift turn on Joe Biden after the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan—voters have just been steadily souring on the president, with corruption as one main reason. (It’s worth noting that, although the FT poll specified that Trump voters are concerned about corruption within the administration, corruption also tops lists because it means different things to different voters. Trump supporters who say they are concerned about “corruption” could be referring, for example, to “deep state” conspiracy theories.) The polling around corruption is also an indication of the success (believe it or not) of much-maligned Democratic messaging. In February, Senator Jon Ossoff began speaking about “the Epstein class,” referring to the then-recent release of materials related to the late sex offender, which sketched a clique of wealthy, powerful people emailing and socializing around the globe. “They are the elites they pretend to hate,” Ossoff said . “Trump was supposed to fight for the working class; instead, he’s literally closing rural clinics and hospitals to cut taxes for George Soros and Elon Musk.” Democrats have been using similar lines ever since . In making “corruption” a rallying cry, Democrats have found a way to yoke together a range of different stories, effectively sidestepping any division between economic issues and Trump scandals. It’s a big enough trend to fit any number of developments: Trump’s promotion of AI and data centers, despite wide public skepticism ; his focus on projects such as the White House ballroom, which is funded by donors, many of whose identities the administration hasn’t disclosed, and an arch in Washington, D.C.; his work to undermine elections. His policy toward Ukraine appears influenced by possible business ventures in Russia. His Iran war was encouraged in part by Middle Eastern allies with whom Trump family members have business relationships. Trump seems determined to help the Democrats out by boasting about oil-company profits at a time when Americans are upset about the cost of filling up their vehicles. Republicans have also bolstered the case with nominees such as Ken Paxton, a one-man alleged-graft spree . If an anti-corruption message does carry Democrats to victory in the House, and perhaps in the Senate, it will also point to how they might use Congress over the next two years. Even if they win both chambers, they will have little ability to enact policy—including actions that might help bring prices down. But a House majority alone would have investigatory power, and could use its reach to delve into Trump-administration actions that threaten both rule of law and voters’ pocketbooks. Related: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption. How corruption got this bad Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : Israeli election results are hazy. When ICE comes for a MAGA supporter What should you do with your money in the age of AI? Today’s News At least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured when a high-speed passenger train rear-ended another train this morning in the province of Toledo, Spain, causing a derailment. Spain’s transportation minister said traffic controllers had inexplicably instructed the train to continue despite another train being stopped farther along the tracks. Israel appears to be headed for a deadlock after its parliamentary election; neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured a clear path to a governing majority. With most votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc is projected to win 53 seats, the opposition 48, and Arab parties a record 19, complicating efforts to form a coalition. The Federal Reserve voted to leave interest rates unchanged despite inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month, driven in part by higher energy prices. Two officials dissented in favor of raising rates, while Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the central bank needed more economic data before deciding whether to increase rates. Evening Read Elizabeth Renstrom for The Atlantic How American Girl Doll Lost Its Way By Hillary Kelly In the early 1990s, when I was in elementary school, a fancy catalog would arrive in the mailbox of our 1950s split-level in Philadelphia four times a year, and I’d hurry to my room to pore over its elaborate spreads. Tea caddies, Windsor chairs, writing quills, ice-cream churns. We didn’t have any antiques in our home, but the lure of the past was so strong that sometimes my sisters, five and seven years older than me, crammed onto my bed to dog-ear the pages too. Most of all, we looked forward to checking in with the girls arrayed there, whose stories we knew so well: Samantha, Molly, Kirsten, Felicity, Addy, and, later in the decade, Josefina. They were the American Girl dolls, preadolescents just slightly older than me, and I was enthralled by the pictures of their period dresses, tiny school supplies, and exotic waxed lunch foods. My own doll was the farm girl Kirsten Larson, a Swedish immigrant to 1850s Minnesota. She had come in a burgundy box, with a slim book titled Meet Kirsten tucked in beside her. I promptly begged for the five other Kirsten books; the historical-fiction series followed the same pattern for each doll, ushering her through a year’s worth of life events, tailored to her personality and time and place. I remember playing with Kirsten in the backyard and having her trace out symbols in the dirt, just as she did with her new friend, a Dakota girl called Singing Bird, in the second book, Kirsten Learns a Lesson . To have such a doll was to own a whole world and the narratives within it … Yet as American Girl’s 40th anniversary arrives, the brand finds itself in something of a midlife crisis. items.title: My generation owes young people mentorship – Kufuor
items.description: Former President John Agyekum Kufuor says his generation owes young people mentorship and should share lessons from its long journey through public life. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said rapid technological change leaves today’s youth little time to follow the lengthy apprenticeship that shaped his career. “So my generation should feel a responsibility to sort of package the experiences we had to go through to get to where we are, because I believe in the intergenerational evolution of society.” Kufuor was responding to a question about young people’s attraction to visible success, including flashy houses and cars, and the journey behind those achievements. He explained that he developed in a slower world. There was time to move from studying law into legal practice, city administration and other responsibilities. “I say I came to what I eventually ended up in through a long apprenticeship. They may not be privileged to undergo such an apprenticeship with time.” With artificial intelligence and other technologies accelerating change, he said older people must make their experience accessible to the next generation. He explained that this responsibility is part of his motivation to leave a legacy through his foundation. Kufuor also challenged assumptions about today’s youth being prepared. He said their education and access to technology give them advantages his generation lacked. “I tend to believe the current generation is far better educated than our generation.” He contrasted today’s access to information through mobile phones with his experience in the 1950s and 1960s, when telephones were scarce even in Kumasi. “They can learn very fast. In that sense, they are better prepared than their ancestors.” For Kufuor, mentorship offers a way to combine those advantages with the practical lessons older generations have acquired. The aim is to help young people gain insights quickly and improve on what their predecessors achieved. The John A. Kufuor Foundation pursues that ambition through its Kufuor Scholars Program. The three-year programme supplements university education with leadership training, mentorship, coaching and practical activities. It seeks to nurture patriotic, ethical and community-minded leaders who can solve problems and contribute to national development. Its activities include leadership camps, internships and personal projects.

items.title: Agro-industrie : Proparco accorde 5 millions d’euros à Soguipal pour porter sa production de yaourt à 15 tonnes par jour
items.description: Le groupe agroalimentaire guinéen Soguipal bénéficie d’un prêt de 5 millions d’euros accordé par Proparco, filiale du groupe Agence française de développement (AFD) dédiée au secteur privé. Ce financement s’inscrit dans un programme d’investissement global de 7,2 millions d’euros, destiné notamment à renforcer les capacités de production de l’entreprise et à soutenir son développement. La convention a été signée le lundi 26 octobre 2026, à la résidence de l’ambassadeur de France en Guinée, après une visite de l’unité de production de BEST Yaourt, située à Sanoyah. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de l’ambassadeur de France en Guinée, Luc Briard, du directeur régional de Proparco pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest, Sadio Dicko, des responsables de Soguipal, ainsi que de plusieurs représentants d’institutions financières et du ministère guinéen chargé de l’Industrie. Cette opération devrait permettre à Soguipal d’accroître sa capacité de production de yaourt de 9 à 15 tonnes par jour, soit une augmentation de près de 67 %. Elle prévoit également la création d’une trentaine d’emplois directs supplémentaires et le financement des besoins en fonds de roulement nécessaires à cette montée en puissance. Un investissement de 7,2 millions d’euros pour accompagner la croissance Prenant la parole lors de la cérémonie, Sadio Dicko a expliqué que le financement de Proparco s’inscrit dans une démarche plus large d’accompagnement des petites et moyennes entreprises guinéennes à fort potentiel. « Le financement que nous scellons ce soir est un prêt de 5 millions d’euros. Il accompagne, de façon plus globale, un programme d’investissement de 7,2 millions d’euros qui permet à Soguipal d’ajouter 6 tonnes de yaourt par jour à sa capacité de production pour atteindre les 15 tonnes quotidiennes », a-t-il déclaré. Au-delà de l’appui financier, Proparco prévoit un programme d’assistance technique visant à renforcer les pratiques opérationnelles de l’entreprise et à améliorer ses processus industriels. Pour Sadio Dicko, cette opération revêt une importance particulière puisqu’elle constitue la première intervention de Proparco en Guinée dans le cadre de son approche « PME en croissance », destinée à accompagner les entreprises nationales présentant de fortes perspectives de développement. Le responsable régional a également salué le parcours entrepreneurial du PDG de Soguipal, Ibrahima Diallo, dont les activités ont débuté en 2005 dans l’importation et la distribution de produits alimentaires, avant de s’orienter vers la transformation industrielle locale. Aujourd’hui, Soguipal fabrique et conditionne notamment du yaourt, du lait en poudre, du concentré de tomates, de la mayonnaise et de la margarine. Ses produits sont distribués par CCG sur le marché guinéen et dans plusieurs pays de la sous-région. Selon Sadio Dicko, avec la marque BEST Yaourt, Soguipal est devenue le seul fabricant industriel de yaourt en Guinée. Soguipal veut renforcer sa présence sur l’ensemble du territoire Du côté de l’entreprise bénéficiaire, ce financement est accueilli comme une nouvelle étape dans sa stratégie de développement. Le directeur administratif et financier du groupe CCG, Aboubacar Baldé, a mis l’accent sur les perspectives industrielles et commerciales ouvertes par cet investissement. « Grâce à ce financement de 5 millions d’euros, notre capacité de production est passée de 9 à 15 tonnes quotidiennement, soit une progression de 67 %, avec la création de 30 emplois supplémentaires directs », a-t-il indiqué. L’entreprise envisage également de développer son réseau logistique à travers la construction progressive de chambres froides et de dépôts de stockage et de distribution dans les différentes régions du pays. Cette stratégie vise à rapprocher les produits des consommateurs tout en améliorant leur conservation et leur disponibilité sur le marché national. Aboubacar Baldé a, par ailleurs, insisté sur les exigences d’hygiène, de sécurité et de protection de l’environnement qui doivent accompagner cette expansion industrielle. « Ce partenariat n’est pas un aboutissement. C’est une nouvelle étape qui nous engage à produire davantage, à créer des emplois, à investir durablement et à contribuer à la souveraineté alimentaire de notre pays », a-t-il souligné. L’ambassadeur de France salue un partenariat tourné vers la production locale Présent à la cérémonie après avoir visité les installations industrielles de Soguipal à Sanoyah, l’ambassadeur de France en Guinée, Luc Briard, a présenté ce financement comme une illustration concrète de la coopération économique entre les deux pays. « Ici, nous illustrons très concrètement la réalité du partenariat entre la France et la Guinée. Un partenariat de confiance, un partenariat durable, de long terme, un partenariat gagnant-gagnant et un partenariat crédible et au service des populations », a-t-il déclaré. Le diplomate français a particulièrement insisté sur la nécessité de développer une industrie capable de répondre aux besoins du marché intérieur. « Vous répondez à un impératif qui vous a été fixé par les autorités guinéennes : produire localement pour le marché local », a-t-il fait remarquer. Luc Briard a également évoqué les perspectives d'approvisionnement de l’entreprise en lait frais provenant de Forécariah. Une initiative qui, si elle se concrétise, pourrait contribuer à renforcer les liens entre les producteurs locaux et les unités industrielles de transformation. Selon lui, le développement de cette filière pourrait également favoriser le désenclavement économique de certaines zones de production et offrir de nouveaux débouchés aux éleveurs guinéens. L’ambassadeur a, en outre, établi un lien entre ce type d’investissement et les ambitions de développement économique portées par le programme Simandou 2040. Un appui salué par le ministère de l’Industrie Représentant le ministre chargé de l’Industrie, Abdoulaye Diallo, chef de cabinet, s’est félicité de la mobilisation de ce financement en faveur d’une entreprise guinéenne. « Voir se concrétiser l’obtention d’un financement de 5 millions d’euros pour une entreprise à fort potentiel dans le domaine de l’agribusiness en Guinée, c’est un motif de satisfaction », a-t-il affirmé. Pour le représentant du département, cet investissement devrait permettre non seulement de renforcer les capacités de production de Soguipal, mais également de soutenir ses besoins de financement à court terme. Il a présenté cette opération comme une illustration des efforts de coopération internationale et de la mise en œuvre des ambitions industrielles du programme Simandou 2040. Réduire la dépendance aux importations de produits laitiers Au-delà du développement de Soguipal, les intervenants ont souligné les enjeux de souveraineté alimentaire liés à cet investissement. Selon les chiffres avancés par Sadio Dicko, la Guinée ne produit localement qu’environ un quart des produits laitiers qu’elle consomme. Le reste provient des importations, exposant le marché national aux fluctuations des prix internationaux et aux contraintes logistiques. Pour Proparco, le renforcement des capacités locales de transformation agroalimentaire constitue ainsi un levier important pour réduire cette dépendance. Le financement accordé à Soguipal s’inscrit également, selon son directeur régional, dans l’initiative FARM, portée par la France en faveur de la sécurité alimentaire, notamment en Afrique. Cette opération illustre par ailleurs la complémentarité recherchée par Proparco entre le financement des banques locales et l’accompagnement direct des entreprises. Sadio Dicko a notamment rappelé le rôle joué par la BCI Guinée, partenaire bancaire historique du groupe Soguipal, dans les échanges ayant conduit à cette intervention. Avec ce nouvel investissement, Soguipal entend désormais franchir une étape supplémentaire dans son développement industriel, renforcer sa présence sur le marché national et consolider ses ambitions dans la sous-région ouest-africaine.

items.title: PLF 2027 : l’opposition juge les mesures de soutien au pouvoir d’achat insuffisantes
items.description: Les groupes de l’opposition à la Chambre des représentants ont apporté leurs remarques et critiques face au projet de loi de finances 2027. Les groupes parlementaire du Parti de la justice et du développement (PJD) et le Mouvement populaire (MP) ont formulé des réserves sur la capacité du PLF à réellement améliorer le pouvoir d’achat, à soutenir l’économie et à répondre aux besoins sociaux. Les groupes de l'opposition ont réagi aux projet de loi de finances en faisant part de leurs remarques qui concernent en premier lieu le pouvoir d’achat, principale préoccupation des députés. Selon eux, les mesures seraient insuffisantes face au coût de la vie. Les députés ont également souligné les limites des hypothèses économiques jugées incertaines notamment concernant le réalisme des prévisions de recettes fiscales. Lors de la réunion de la Commission des finances et du développement économique de la Chambre, tenue ce mercredi, le groupe du Parti de la justice et du développement (PJD) a estimé que les mesures censées soutenir le pouvoir d'achat ne garantissaient pas cette finalité, notamment en ce qui concerne les exonérations fiscales, les dispositifs de soutien à la consommation et les augmentations de salaires et de pensions. Driss Al Azami El Idrissi, président du groupe, a expliqué que la répartition des crédits entre les secteurs et l’annonce de budgets supplémentaires pour l’éducation, la santé et d’autres domaines ne suffisaient pas, à elles seules, à clarifier la politique économique du gouvernement. Selon lui, il est nécessaire que le gouvernement approfondisse et précise les choix qui guideront l’intervention de l’État, les modalités de coordination entre les politiques budgétaire et monétaire et la politique de change, ainsi que la nature des relations avec le secteur privé et le système bancaire. De son côté, le groupe parlementaire du Mouvement populaire a relevé des incohérences entre les hypothèses et prévisions économiques contenues dans le PLF 2027 et les réalités mondiales, mettant en avant les incertitudes géopolitiques, les risques de hausse des prix du pétrole et du gaz butane, et l’augmentation du coût du service de la dette publique. A travers sa présidente, Rim Chabat, le groupe du MP a souligné la baisse des crédits alloués au Fonds de compensation, qui passent de 22 milliards de dirhams en 2026 à 19,4 milliards, en relevant le contexte de la hausse du coût de la vie et la pression sur les ménages. Le groupe du Mouvement populaire a également estimé que les effets de la réforme de l’impôt sur le revenu seraient limités, et a appelé à prendre des mesures urgentes pour endiguer le phénomène de spéculation et la multiplication des intermédiaires sur les marchés des produits alimentaires. Sur le même volet, le groupe du PJD s’est interrogé sur le réalisme des prévisions ayant servi à élaborer le projet de loi de finances, notamment en ce qui concerne l’augmentation attendue des recettes fiscales. Dans ce sens, il a appelé le ministre de l’Économie et des Finances et de l’Efficacité publique à expliquer la méthodologie retenue pour calculer ces ressources. © Mounir Mehimdate Le Mouvement populaire a appelé à mettre en place des mesures de protection accompagnant toute hausse des impôts sur les entreprises du secteur des hydrocarbures, afin, selon le groupe d'opposition, d’éviter que ces augmentations ne se répercutent par des charges supplémentaires subies pour les consommateurs. Le PJD a évoqué les entreprises et établissements concernés par les opérations de privatisation, appelant à la publication de leurs noms, soulignant que ces entités dont le gouvernement attend des recettes, devraient être connues. Le groupe parlementaire a ainsi appelé à partager les informations sur ces entités concernées et les mécanismes retenus pour les opérations de privatisation. Enfin, sur la question du pouvoir d'achat, le groupe de la Lampe a demandé au gouvernement de préciser et spécifier ce qu'il entendait par des prévisions de retours à des prix « raisonnables et normaux ». Il a demandé à expliquer les critères qui seront utilisés pour déterminer un retour à des prix normaux, tout en estimant que les citoyens attendent des prix inférieurs à ceux pratiqués ces dernières années et des mesures concrètes. The post PLF 2027 : l’opposition juge les mesures de soutien au pouvoir d’achat insuffisantes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Northern Ashanti Mines: Former chief inspector of mines urges Minerals Commission to negotiate over debt
items.description: A former Chief Inspector of Mines with the Minerals Commission, Obiri Yeboah Twumasi, has urged the Commission to negotiate a payment plan with Northern Ashanti Mines over its alleged outstanding statutory fees rather than allow the dispute to escalate. He says a negotiated settlement could help the company meet its financial obligations while continuing to develop its mine, particularly as it is yet to begin production and generate revenue from gold sales. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story , Mr Twumasi said that where the alleged breaches relate to statutory payments, the Commission and the company should consider an arrangement that allows the outstanding amounts to be paid over an agreed period. “But if the current breaches are to do with statutory payments, I think they can sit down and resolve it and a payment plan established by the company to the acceptance of the Minerals Commission for them to pay,” he said. Mr Twumasi explained that a mining company still constructing its processing plant and investing in equipment may not have sufficient cash flow to meet its financial obligations, leaving it dependent on suppliers and creditors to sustain its operations. He said the Minerals Commission should therefore exercise caution in handling the matter, while the company must also be mindful of its obligations. His comments come amid a dispute over the revocation of Northern Ashanti Mines’ licence, with the Minerals Commission reportedly claiming that the company owes more than US$8.38 million in statutory fees. Mr Twumasi also stressed that the Commission must follow the prescribed procedures when dealing with alleged breaches by mining companies. Read also: Northern Ashanti Mines challenges Minerals Commission over Konongo takeover, disputes $8.3m debt He said the Commission should notify a company of any serious breaches and give it 120 days to remedy them. If the issues remain unresolved, he said, a further 120-day period should be granted. “The Minerals Commission should notify the company, give them 120 days in the first instance for them to remedy any breaches that probably they might have notified them. If after the 120 days, a second window is open for the company, another 120 days is given to the company for them to remedy any breaches,” he said. Mr Twumasi called on both parties to resolve their differences through dialogue, arguing that a prolonged dispute would not serve the interests of the country. “What we need to do is for two sides to sit down and negotiate whatever differences that they have. So that at the end of the day, the benefit will inure to the whole country,” he added.

items.title: Bolsonaro claims he is Brazil’s true leader after fleeing to US
items.description: Brazil’s defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro insisted Wednesday he is his country’s rightful leader after arriving in the United States to start a self-imposed exile. Bolsonaro’s defiance on fleeing to Florida signaled continued upheaval for Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a dramatic runoff election Sunday. “I am the elected president, and the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny,” Bolsonaro said in the statement published on his X account, slamming “electoral fraud.” “I will lead the opposition from here,” he said. In a subsequent statement, he revised his claim, saying he is the “leader,” rather than “president.” Bolsonaro, 45, touched down earlier Wednesday in a private jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami. President Donald Trump’s hard-right administration has strong links to Bolsonaro and his father Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brazil after attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022. Trump reiterated his stand that Brazil’s election was “very strange” but told reporters he “won’t get involved” in Flavio Bolsonaro’s claim to the presidency. Details of how Bolsonaro, accompanied by his wife and daughters, made it to US soil are still emerging. He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering. With his current parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports but left anyway, reaching the United States via Argentina and Ecuador. A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro’s Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, according to Italian documents seen by AFP. The US Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared “with applicable immigration laws and procedures.” The travel ban was issued by powerful Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against Flavio Bolsonaro’s father and is a controversial figure hated by the Brazilian right. Flavio Bolsonaro had vowed to seek the justice’s impeachment if he were elected — which up until Lula’s comeback in the runoff had looked increasingly likely. – ‘Shameful’ act – Lula, who won the election with 51.8 percent of Sunday’s vote, called Flavio Bolsonaro’s departure a “shameful” act. “A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide,” he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration on Tuesday. But Brazil police issued a statement Wednesday saying that he was not considered a fugitive. There was controversy in neighboring Argentina, where opposition lawmakers demanded to know how Bolsonaro had managed to transit through the country. While Argentinian authorities said he was carrying valid travel documents, officials have requested chief of cabinet Diego Santilli to provide details to parliament, according to opposition lawmaker Agustin Rossi. – Fraud cases – The most high-profile fraud case against Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil centers on the unreleased biopic “Dark Horse” starring US actor Jim Caviezel as Flavio’s father Jair. In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately $24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil’s biggest-ever fraud cases. Before the leak, Flavio Bolsonaro had denied knowing Vorcaro, or that he had financed the movie. In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the financing of the film, and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency. Flavio Bolsonaro acknowledged Vorcaro had funded the film, but insisted it was a private business deal that was “completely legal.” In another probe, police are investigating whether Flavio Bolsonaro laundered money and moved funds out of the country in collaboration with his close friend, the lawyer Willer Tomaz. Flavio’s father Jair Bolsonaro also never conceded defeat after losing to Lula and left the country on the eve of his rival’s inauguration, before returning to Brazil three months later. AFP The post Bolsonaro claims he is Brazil’s true leader after fleeing to US appeared first on Vanguard News .
