Si nous pensons qu’il est acceptable d’arracher des enfants à leurs parents ou de supprimer des programmes destinés aux personnes âgées ou aux personnes fragiles, afin que les puissants puissent obtenir tout ce qu’ils veulent, nous continuerons à croupir dans la colère et la division. Et je ne sais pas pour vous, mais j’en ai assez d’être en colère. Et j’en ai assez d’être divisé. Je veux tendre la main à mon voisin et lui serrer la main. Je veux me mettre au travail pour faire quelque chose pour quelqu’un d’autre. Nous ne sommes pas arrivés à cette situation du jour au lendemain. Nous n’en sortirons pas du jour au lendemain. Et aucun d’entre nous ne devrait prétendre qu’une seule personne, à un poste quelconque, va d’une manière ou d’une autre nous sauver la mise, et que le reste d’entre nous peut simplement recommencer à agir comme avant. Nous allons tous devoir changer certaines choses. Mais Ohio, voici ce que je sais. Cette élection peut être un début. Cette élection peut être un tournant. Cette élection peut être un changement de cap dans le long parcours de l’Amérique vers une union plus parfaite. Car si nous sommes prêts à nous mobiliser en masse ici, dans l’Ohio, et dans tout le pays, si nous sommes prêts à voter pour le changement, et à voter pour les démocrates à tous les niveaux, alors cette élection pourrait bien marquer le moment où ce pays a commencé à s’engager dans une meilleure direction. Lorsque nous laissons derrière nous nos pires pulsions et que nous commençons à aligner notre politique sur nos idéaux les plus élevés, rien n’arrête un changement dont l’heure est venue. Vous et moi Ohio, nous l’avons déjà prouvé. Dans dix jours, vous aurez l’occasion de le faire à nouveau. Alors, je vous le demande : êtes-vous motivés ? Êtes-vous prêts à vous lancer ? Faisons d’Amy Acton la gouverneure. Faisons de Sherrod Brown le sénateur. Engageons-nous sur la voie qui mènera à une Amérique meilleure. Merci, je vous aime. Que Dieu vous bénisse. Que Dieu bénisse les États-Unis d’Amérique. L’article Obama contre Trump : « Nous devons redresser notre boussole morale » est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: The Man Who Risked Death Documenting ISIS
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with thoughts on the coming midterm elections and the difficult position Republicans now face. He explains the political “fork” confronting Republican candidates: Having attached themselves to an unpopular president, they risk alienating either moderate voters or Trump’s loyal base. Then David is joined by Omar Mohammed, the formerly anonymous blogger behind Mosul Eye, to discuss his new book, Mosul Eye: A Scholar’s Clandestine War Against ISIS . They discuss life under ISIS rule, the atrocities Mohammed witnessed firsthand in Mosul, and the dangers he faced in documenting them. Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of the role opera plays in our society. The following is a transcript of the episode: Omar Mohammed: Our city was taken by the Islamic State, David, because we had no memory of anything that happened before. Because we allowed other people to be omitted. I don’t put blame on people collectively. That’s not what I do. That’s not my job. That’s not my craft. But my craft is also to understand why what happened happened. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Omar Mohammed, a historian and author of the harrowing new book Mosul Eye, an eyewitness account of the ISIS reign of terror in the city of Mosul, Iraq. The book talk at the end of the show will not be about books at all. This week, I’m going to be offering some meditations on the place of opera in our culture. But before either the dialogue with Omar Mohammed or the meditation on opera, some opening thoughts about something that has been puzzling me as we come to the end of the 2026 race, and maybe has been puzzling you as well. As we all know, President Trump is in a lot of political trouble. He’s polling in the mid-30s: about where President [George W.] Bush was polling just before the big beating in the midterm elections of 2006, about where President Harry Truman was polling before the big Democratic beating in the elections of 1946. One thing you might expect in a situation like this, where the president’s unpopularity is dragging down his party, is that individual members of the president’s party would try to look independent—put some distance between themselves and the president—in order to say, Look, maybe you’re mad at him , but don’t be mad at me . I did a good job for the people of my state, my district. Separate me out. Just don’t mix me in with Trump. Why are you mixing me in with Trump? I’m different. I’ve disagreed with him. I’m independent. And you’re seeing very, very little of that kind of behavior. And the question is, why? Why won’t Republicans try to save themselves by putting some distance between them and Trump? It’s maybe late as we get into the second half of October. Why didn’t they do it before? The explanation comes from a strategy in the game of chess. If you play chess, you are familiar with a maneuver called a fork. A fork is a tactic in which a single piece attacks two or more of the opponent’s pieces at the same time, forcing the opponent into a situation where the opponent can save only one of the threatened pieces. Republicans are in kind of this situation in this election of 2026. Yes, President Trump is unpopular. But in many places, especially in red states, the hope of survival is not by distancing from Trump but by somehow getting Republican turnout inflated to rev up the Republican base. And the way you do that is by clinging to President Trump, because as little as the rest of the country likes President Trump, his base continues to like him enthusiastically. The base is shrinking. There are fewer and fewer people who describe themselves as MAGA Republicans. But among those who do describe themselves as MAGA Republicans—and that’s a considerable number of people—the president’s support remains overwhelming, almost unanimous. So if you’re a Republican in a state like Iowa or Florida or even Texas, you’re in a situation where you think, I need to do two things. I need to find some way to bring independents back, and that requires distance from President Trump. But I need to make sure that my people, our people, turn up, and that requires clinging to President Trump. In other words, a classic fork. And this fork is creating a kind of paralysis that may make the Republican situation in 2026 worse even than it has to be. Because instead of winning both independents and revving up the base, the Republicans caught in the fork may find themselves doing neither and collapsing in places that always had been thought about as winnable. And where this may have real consequences for the American political system and for the next two years is less in the Senate, less in the House, and more at a part of American politics that we tend not to think about as a system—we tend to think only about our own state—and that is the politics of the states. A defining feature of American politics almost for the entire past generation has been the overwhelming dominance of the Republicans at the state level, and especially at the state-legislative level. There are 99 state legislatures, because Nebraska has only one chamber. So, 50 states; two chambers per state, except in Nebraska, you get to 99. Of those 99, Republicans have had, through most of the 21st century, an enormous majority almost all of the time. Sometimes a little more, sometimes a little less, but always they can bank on great control at the state level. And that’s had a lot of implications, because it has been the secret weapon behind President Trump’s concentration of power at the federal level. When Trump was trying to manipulate the elections of 2020 and hold onto power in 2021 after his defeat, one of the things he had going for him is a lot of the places where the opposition to Trump might coalesce at the state level, that didn’t happen. And states often let President Trump get away with doing things that—if they were under non-Trump control, or if there was an even more even division of the parties—they would not allow. The trouble that Republicans are in in 2026 could have big implications for state contests. Could perhaps even break the Republican majority on state legislatures, break the Republican hold on so many governor’s races. And this will have, for the final two years of President Trump’s term and for the 2028 election, implications as large as the opposite had in the first term of President Trump and in the election of 2020. He may be facing in 2028, or his party may be facing in 2028, a state system that is much more independent of the federal system than it has been before, and much less amenable to the kind of manipulation and tricks that Trump tried in 2020 and that led to the January 6th, 2021, attack on Congress. If the Republican power subsides at the state level, Republicans will face another problem as well, and one with even longer-term consequences for the renewal of their party. Oftentimes, when parties are beaten at the federal level—as it looks probable that the Republicans will be beaten in 2026, and as it looks very questionable that they will survive in 2028—they find renewal at the state level. And the classic example of this is the career of the president I wrote speeches for, George W. Bush. In the 1990s Republicans in Congress and Senate sought to impeach President Bill Clinton. This move was tremendously unpopular and led to very bad Republican results in the midterm election of 1998 and to the resignation of then–Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. George W. Bush, in the same year, 1998, where Republicans did bad in congressional elections, George W. Bush won a decisive re-election as governor of Texas, with important breakthroughs in winning the Hispanic vote. And Republicans all over the country looked and said, Well, the people in Washington, the Republicans in Washington, they don’t seem to know what they’re doing. But this Republican in Texas—he seems to have the formula. And Bush began his campaign for the nomination in 2000 after that breakthrough in 1998 by presenting himself as a different kind of Republican. Different from whom? Different from Newt Gingrich, different from the people who’d impeached Bill Clinton. And so the result was that he could reinvent himself, reinvent his party. And the unsuccessful election of 1998 was followed by renewal in time for the election of the year 2000. How do the Republicans do that post-Trump? They can’t, because they are caught in the fork. I mean, one thing you might imagine, for example, is that instead of nominating J. D. Vance or even Marco Rubio in 2028—someone closely tied with everything that Americans don’t like about Donald Trump—Republicans would say to themselves, Well, is there a state that’s an important state, a contested state, where there’s a governor who’s very popular? What do you know? There is one. Georgia is that contested state, and Georgia has an outgoing governor, Brian Kemp, who’s had ratings of over 60 percent for much of his second term, who’s polling at about 60 percent right now, and who has done a good job of straddling the division between Republicans who don’t like Trump and Republicans who do. That’s the guy, you would think. That’s the guy. That’s our George W. Bush. That’s the guy who can break with Trump, be a Republican, be a different kind of Republican. Different from whom? Different from Trump. He doesn’t like Trump, but he’s still a Republican. But that’s not happening, is it? It’s not happening, because Republican Party politics since 1998 has been effectively nationalized. It’s all Trump all the time; all federal, not state. And that not only defeats the attempts by Republicans at the national level to perform shenanigans; it also denies Republicans the chance to renew themselves from the place where, in American politics, renewal so often comes at the state level. That’s a fork. It’s a fork the Republicans are not finding their way out of, and it’s a fork that will have large tactical consequences in 2026 and maybe large strategic consequences in 2028. And now, my dialogue with Omar Mohammed. [ Music ] Frum: In June 2014, the armies of the Islamic State seized Mosul, Iraq’s second city. Not long after, an anonymous blog called Mosul Eye began reporting on life inside the occupied city. The executions, the expulsions of Christians and Shiites, the mass rape of Yazidi girls, the destruction of shrines and manuscripts. For more than three years, no one outside a tiny circle knew who was writing it. Journalists relied on it, and the Islamic State threatened its author with death in its most terrible forms. In December 2017, after Mosul was retaken, the Associated Press revealed the writer’s identity. His name was Omar Mohammed, a young historian of Ottoman Mosul. Omar Mohammed lived a double life, outwardly conforming to ISIS edicts by day and recording the truth of what was happening to his city by night, until he fled the city at the end of 2015 and continued from abroad through a network of contacts inside Mosul. His brother was killed in the final battle to liberate the city. He has now told the full story in his own words in a new book, Mosul Eye: A Scholar’s Clandestine War Against ISIS , published by Skyhorse Press. It is, in my opinion, a work of literature about the human spirit, to stand on the shelf with Primo Levi and Czesław Miłosz. A witness to the extremes of human cruelty, oppression, and endurance. Omar Mohammed, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show . Omar Mohammed: David, thank you for having me, and I’m humbled by the words you said about me and about the book. Frum: I think anyone in your presence understands the courage that you showed. Your life is a rebuke to all of us of what it means to be brave, not in a dangerous second, but through the grind of minute-by-minute exposure to terror and oppression and the risk of death. I want to talk to you about your book. For, as a book and as a witness, because the book, as I said in the introduction, is also, in my opinion, a great work of literature. It’s not just a testimony. It is a work of creative understanding of what people have gone through. But before we talk about any of those things, let me just start with this. As you know, you spend some time in the United States now. It’s a very busy country, a very inward-looking country, a very forgetful country. You’re a historian. You devoted your career and then the risk of death to remembrance. Why is it important to remember what happened in your city in those years? Mohammed: There are two ways of saying that also, David. It’s not just why we should remember, but also why we should not forget. Because I’ve always said I can forgive, but forgetting is dangerous. The reason being, the past 30 to 40 years that witnessed the rise of the so-called jihad on the West or jihad on democracy, against democracy, it believes in only one objective and one outcome and one goal. And that is the destruction of the Western democracy and Western civilization. They stand against everything democracy stands for. We should never forget. We should never stop remembering that they are always planning and plotting against the Western democracy and against the West in general. And this is a way of life that they don’t think should exist, and that they believe it must be eliminated and destroyed. So yes, it’s a fight, and it’s my task as a historian to keep reminding the people, Westerners or non-Westerners. Because, trust me, if the Western democracy is removed, no one is going to be safe, and that is exactly what they want. We should always fight back. That is my act of remembrance, and that is why I want people to always remember. Frum: And you continue through your activism, but you also continue as a historian trying to recapture the past of what Mosul was like before ISIS, and what life was like during ISIS. I want to read from your book one of the most terrible and vivid scenes of what you saw as a witness to history. You have, in this part of the book, you have entered the ISIS capital in Syria. You are approaching from the outskirts, and you see a man who has literally been crucified, like Jesus in the Bible. You say, “In front of it was a man nailed to a cross”—you say you’re in front of an abandoned school. “In front of it was a man nailed to a cross. He was mounted in the manner described in the scriptures: arms extended, nails through the hands, the body suspended above the ground. A piece of paper bearing his name was attached to his chest: Sulyman Ayub . The charge was apostasy, the accusation that a Muslim had abandoned his faith, one of the offenses ISIS published with the most theatrical severity. The word for death was written beneath it in Arabic. But the man was not dead. He was moving, the small involuntary shifts of a living person in agony. Below him, dogs were feeding on his legs. Not strays circling at a distance, but animals that had been allowed to reach the body and were eating from it while the man lived.” That’s a terrible scene. You give us the man’s name, and you were the only witness to his terrible end and the reasons for it. Mohammed: I’m sorry, David, because you just read something to me that I thought by writing I will. I heard that—I wish you did not read this text. Frum: I’m sorry. Mohammed: I just did not want— Frum: I wish I had not read it either, but I have and I did because of you. Mohammed: Yes. And you can imagine I saw that man on my way of escaping the Islamic State. I made sure that I read his name. I made sure that I record his name. I made sure I protect his name from being forgotten. I also made sure by naming him, by giving him that name, that hopefully will outlast me and outlive me, but it will definitely outlive the Islamic State. That people will know that the people who were killed by the Islamic State had names, they had dreams. But it’s also—that animalistic nature of the Islamic State has unfortunately been on many occasions being read or being treated as, Well, what if the Islamic State is just a political movement trying to regain power in its area of interest? That is absolutely absurd. The Islamic State does not use violence to achieve its goals. It uses violence because that is the end goal of its ideology. And this is one scene, David. Not to mention what’s across the book. I just wanted people to know that those people had names, and they should never be forgotten. Frum: Well, I hope I won’t upset you. I want to read—I’m going to be reading some more things from the book as we go, to sort of root us so [that] people can also understand what you have done. And this book, you told me, was originally written in English. It is not translated. Mohammed: It’s in English, yes. Frum: One of your acts of courageous witness was to masquerade as a doctor or a medical professional to gain entrance to the hospitals, to see what was going on inside the hospitals. And you tell this story. In this case, I think you were not an eyewitness. I think you had interviewed somebody. This is from page 116: “Yazidi girls, members of an ancient ethno-religious minority from the Sinjar region, whom ISIS had enslaved en masse the previous summer, were being brought in by ISIS fighters requesting mandatory abortions and sterilizations.” That is, the fighters were demanding mandatory abortions and sterilizations. “The doctor,” to whom you were speaking, “described a girl of 17 who had been raped repeatedly by multiple men and was in a state of nervous collapse. The girl refused the procedure.” That is, I assume, sterilization. “The number of such cases at that point was between 50 and 60. At least 12 girls younger than 15 had died of injuries from the violence. I wrote it down that evening in the same compressed register I use for everything: date, location, number, source. I’m not sure I’ve ever found the right language for what it takes to apply that method to that material. I wrote it down because if I did not, it would disappear into the silence ISIS was building around everything it did to Yazidi women.” Mohammed: I remember this very well. I remember what the doctor told me, but I also equally remember the three other young girls that were killed and shot dead by the Islamic State. As we speak today, and as I mentioned, exactly what you say—that I write it so people will remember. So they will not be forgotten. Today in 2026, we have people questioning that even the heinous attack against the Yazidis even took place or even happened. People are denying or questioning, or people are trying to make it look like, well, we were all attacked. Why does it have to be special for the Yazidis? Because that is the risk. If we do not record what the Islamic State did, there will be other people who will come and say, they will say that it was not that bad. It was not that horrible. And that will always—as a historian, that is always the challenge. Because as historians, we are supposed to deal with the dead. But what I wanted to do is to give life to those people who were killed, so they will be forever witnesses to what happened to them. Frum: My colleague at The Atlantic, Anne Applebaum, a great scholar of the Stalinist and communist oppression in Eastern Europe, wrote in the preface—I’m going to now forget which of her books she wrote this, I think it was maybe her book on the Gulag, the Soviet Gulag. She said, “I write this book”—I’m quoting from memory—“not so that it will never happen again, but because it will happen again.” And I think one of the things I am reminded of by you and by, as I say, the other people I imagine you standing beside on the shelf, Primo Levi and Czesław Miłosz, of just these horrors occur again and again and again. And the only remedy against them—not the remedy, the way of beginning a remedy—is through unceasing remembrance. Mohammed: Our city was taken by the Islamic State, David, because we had no memory of anything that happened before. Because we allowed other people to be omitted. I don’t put blame on people collectively. That’s not what I do. That’s not my job. That’s not my craft. But my craft is also to understand why what happened happened. When the Islamic State took control of [a] third of Iraq and also over [a] third of Syria—but as much as I’m concerned with the city of Mosul, which is my hometown that I unfortunately lost forever, we had no memory of what happened before. We had no memory of what happened to the Jews in the ’40s and the ’50s. We had no memory of what happened to the Assyrians in the ’50s, all of these massacres. We had no memory of what happened in the ’50s. We had no memory of what happened in the early 2000s. People unfortunately forget, David. That’s why it is easy. It’s easy to take control of their past, present, and future. And it was my job to precisely make sure that, because as you cited Anne Applebaum, yes—I do completely agree that it might happen again. My job—I might not be able to prevent it, but if it happens again, at least there will not be only one person to fight against them. But everyone will be prepared, will be ready to understand what they are and what they represent. Frum: I want to put an asterisk beside something you said a few moments ago. You referred to what happened to the Jews in the ’40s and ’50s, and many North American listeners, many English-speaking people, will think you’re meaning about the Nazi Holocaust in Europe. But you’re actually speaking about events that happened to the Jews in Iraq. Mohammed: That’s exactly what I was referring to: the pogrom in Baghdad in the ’40s, or known as the Farhud. But also the revocation of the citizenship, the deportation of the Jews, confiscation of their properties and lands. There is an ancient Jewish history in Iraq that was completely omitted to the extent that I myself had no idea until I grew up, until I started finding out on my own. I had no idea that we had Jews in Mosul. I had no idea that the school I used to attend was built on the ruins of a Jewish school that was completely demolished to the ground. Of course, that allows people to be okay with things to happen again and again. Frum: Well, you both judge people, but you’re very humane in your judgments of the choices and options that are available to ordinary people. And I want to read another passage here—this is from page 65 and 66—because, look: Americans may remember the fight over Mosul, which was spearheaded by American troops with their Iraqi troops, their other coalition forces. And it was a terrible battle, and we had images from it, but not from inside. There was a very effective censorship. And it’s easy to see the people who are in that city as just part of the scenery, part of the story, and you bring this extraordinary sympathy to them. And I want to read again from your book, page 65, 66: “The population of an occupied city does not divide into resistors and collaborators. That is the binary of people who have never lived under total control. The reality is a spectrum so compressed that the distance between cooperation and refusal can be measured in the angle at which a man places money on a counter. A father who sent his son to the rewritten school”—that is, ISIS had taken command of the schools, and it foisted this reactionary curriculum on them—“a father who sent his son to the rewritten school was not endorsing ISIS’s curriculum. He was calculating that a distorted education was less damaging than no education at all, and that a boy seen on the streets during school hours would attract the attention of the Hisba, the religious police. A shopkeeper who paid the zakat , the forced tribute, was not funding the caliphate by conviction. He was buying another day of operation with the only currency the regime accepted. A woman who wore the niqab was not submitting to the ideology. She was navigating a city in which her uncovered face was a punishable offense and her covered face was survival. These were not moral failures. They were the daily calculations of prisoners performing the routines that captors required in order to remain alive.” Mohammed: And I believe that’s exactly how we need to look at people whose will was stripped away. They were under total control of such a brutal regime. There is another way of resistance that I had noted back then, because you mentioned the curricula and the schools. There is, in another page in the book, when the professors of the university were forced to sit inside the library that ISIS had occupied and transformed into its hub to rewrite the curricula before they destroy the library. Those professors—they knew that if they say no, they will be killed, they will be punished. But they at least decided to take some act of resistance. Even if it’s unnoticeable; even if it’s only for themselves to notice. Which is what they did, David. They would start writing slower and slower, slowly, slowly. So what is supposed to be delivered in one week, they would deliver it in two months, because they were always in the hope—probably in one month that ISIS would be removed, ISIS would disappear. So they would just go back to themself and say, I delayed them. I did not give them what they want quickly. So there were people who would take this type of act of resistance. I actually prepared back then an entire confidential report, which I called “The Civil Disobedience,” because I needed to understand what might be the way to get into the people in case there will be a need to form a military resistance against the Islamic State. What do I need? Because I had thought about this. I don’t believe in violence. I don’t believe in such actions. But I needed to understand the mentality of the people. That’s why I went to go deeper inside the mentality of the people. And as you said—yes, we have to be human. Frum: Iraq is a land of fathomless antiquity. Cities are built on top of cities. Mosul, your Mosul, is the city that Bible readers will know as Nineveh. I mean, it’s got a much more ancient history than that, but it is the city to which the prophet Jonah was sent. And the shrine to the prophet Jonah figures largely in your book. Tell us about this layered history: Christian, Jewish, pre-Islamic, Islamic, Ottoman, modern. You are a historian. You describe a city that is built on layers and where the palaces of Assyrian kings from ancient Assyria are still there to be seen. Mohammed: I will start with a joke that goes on until today in Mosul related to Jonah. So the people of Nineveh—as you mentioned, Mosul is across the river from Nineveh. Which is the capital of the Assyrian Empire, which was destroyed in the year 612 B.C. by the Medes and the Babylonians. And since then, the city of Mosul, which also existed back then, became more prominent, as the Assyrians kept moving to the other side. But also has the story of Jonah—and in the Bible it’s the fish, in the Quran it’s the whale, or it’s a big fish. And he arrived in Nineveh, and he started asking them to accept his message. And the joke goes—which is actually not a joke, but the people use it to say that we are the only people who were divinely protected. They say when God asked the people of Nineveh to accept his message, they told him, Give us your offer. Come back in three days; we’ll think about it. And he would come back in three days, and then they would say, Now we have contemplated; we can accept the offer. And then they were given a divine protection forever. And that’s how people grew up in Mosul. That’s how I learned this story, from my grandmother telling me that we are the people of Yunus. We were never told that we are the people of the caliphate. We are—Yunus, it is the Arabic name—one of the names of the city of Mosul is “the city of Jonah.” And you have this layer, and then you have an ancient Assyrian palace on top of that first layer. And then on top of the ancient Assyrian site, which has been rediscovered again, you have an ancient synagogue. And then on top of which a church was built, on top of which a tomb was built, on top of which a mosque was built. That’s how Mosul is. It’s a multilayered city. It’s as contradictory, as beautiful at once. Frum: And Mosul is bisected by the River Tigris. And on one side is a more ancient city—an Ottoman city, I suppose. And on the other side is a more modern city with wider streets and more modern buildings. And this duality is a central feature of the book. Mohammed: Yes. Because that is exactly what you see, and that’s exactly why I care a lot about the river. You can stand in the middle of the river. You look at the right, you see the modernity, you see modern life. But then you look at the left—everything is ancient. Wherever you step on, this is ancient. This is the oldest church in Mosul. This is the oldest synagogue. This is the oldest mosque. This is the oldest street. This is the oldest alley. Everything you mention there, you must add that first word: It’s the oldest. And wherever you step, you are surrounded by history. You are surrounded by complex history, I would say. Because also, as much as Mosul is old and ancient, it also has multilayered society. Different religions, different faiths. But it’s also a city that has never been able to have this as a merged society. This is why we have always had in the city, what you have as the Jewish quarter or the Christian quarter or the Islamic quarter. People did not mix. But they always found a way to mix where it brought them together—which is the old market. And it can continue to live. Frum: I’m going to read one last thing, a very vivid description of the end when the coalition forces came to expel ISIS from Mosul. The Tigris is spanned by bridges. The coalition blew up the bridges, all but one, in order to sever the ability of ISIS to move fighters from one side to the other. ISIS then blew up, you say, the last of the bridges in order to fortify itself. And the more modern part of the city was cleared with considerable violence, but still leaving the city substantially intact. And at that point, the fight turned to the older part of the city. And here’s what you say about that. “The West Mosul”—the West Mosul is the older part—“the West Mosul offensive was set for February 19th, 2017. What was coming would be unlike anything the city had endured in its thousands of years of continuous habitation. Not the Mongol sack of the 13th century, not the Ottoman conquests, not the British mandate, not even the fall to ISIS. What was coming was the destruction of Mosul by the forces that had come to save it. The old city, the city of shared walls and narrow alleys, and the leaning minaret, and the churches beside the mosques, and the shrines beside the markets, was about to be fed into the machinery of liberation. And the machinery did not distinguish between the enemy and the place the enemy had chosen to die inside. The time had come to end ISIS. The price of ending it was Mosul.” Mohammed: It is the price we paid, David. Mosul in its total shape, in its total history. Mosul, that still holds the body of my brother, is the price we paid, yes. But it’s the price we paid, and I’m willing to pay this price again if ISIS comes back again. I’m sorry. [ Cries .] I did not expect myself today to—yeah, we paid Mosul as the price to end that totalitarian, brutal Islamist regime that came for the destruction of every memory we have built. Of every dream we had. Of every stone we marked, was completely erased. But it was a price worth paying, and I would give myself, and I would do it again. And I’m going to give 1,000 Mosul to ensure that no Islamic State, no caliphate would ever see the light. 1,000 Mosul, not one. Frum: You did often put your life at risk, and at one point in a moment of gloom, you shaved your beard, you put on a red sweater. Red was prohibited for some reason I don’t understand. And you sort of walked around and waited for them to find you, and they didn’t. After you made good your escape—and this is a strange thing about the modern world—ISIS has cast Mosul back into what we would call medieval barbarity, although it was much worse than anything that ever happened in the Middle Ages. And yet you’re able to be in contact with your family inside the city. And especially your brother, to whom you were so close, and you lose him in that last fight. Mohammed: I insisted. I insisted on him. I kept telling him. I told him, This is not a warning I am giving you to leave where you are. I’m not telling you that I expect there is going to be a fight there. I’m telling you that I know that the fight is moving into the area where you are, and you must leave now. I did not know I was talking to a dead person. I think my brother realized he was dead. I think he understood. Because my brother, back then when he was talking to me, he was very calm. He was very sincere. He had the serenity that I have never seen before, because he is the one who was always concerned with our safety. He was always concerned, myself, my family, caring for us. But that time he was serene, he was calmer. My brother did not survive. The next day I knew. I knew that the moment I was talking to him, I knew he’s already dead. I knew he was a dead man, and I knew that he knew he was a dead man I just could not save my brother. It is one of my greatest regrets that I couldn’t—I should have, I should have kept calling him. I should have kept calling him. I should have sent someone to remove him from that area. I just, I couldn’t. Frum: You lived this strange life in exile where you were once totally helpless and yet also quite powerful. Because your information was being fed into the global system that was monitoring what ISIS was doing, that was informing the forces that were gathering to destroy ISIS. You could see, but you couldn’t touch what was going on in your city. And you could target, you could assist the coalition forces in targeting death, but you could not save anybody. Mohammed: Yes. I could not just give up. I could not stand and do nothing. I realized that I had the power of saving people. It was a very difficult decision to do, because it meant that I will have to be in contact with the coalition, be in contact with the Central Command. Be in contact with people that I’ve always resisted responding to. But when I realized that I had the tools that allowed me to save more lives. There were people getting killed on [a] daily basis, whether it’s by ISIS or the bombing or—it’s a battlefield. An irregular war, taking place in one of the oldest cities in the world, in which if you, not bombing a house, if you push too hard on the wall, the house is going to collapse. People were desperate. I found the tools, I understood how it works. I used my presence in Paris back then, with that access to technology. And as I mentioned in my book, my brother I did not save, I couldn’t save. I saved 92 families, and I am always thankful that they are alive. I am always devastated that others could not make it. But I do remember that at least those lives were saved. At least others are still alive. Frum: Let me ask you about your life in the past 10 years. So the fight for Mosul is over in 2017. ISIS is expelled. The city is wrecked. Your identity is revealed at the end of 2017 by the Associated Press. You have now made a life; you’ve returned to your teaching and research work, and you spend your time in Paris and other cities. What is your work like? What is your mission like in the 10 years since the book’s story comes to an end? Mohammed: After I escaped and the moment I arrived in safety in France, I did not stop working on doing whatever I can to help the city. When it was the battle, I used every tool available to me to help the people. And then the biggest challenge came, which is the recovery of the city. I started immediately advocating for resupplying the central library of the city of Mosul with books. People were asking, What do you want? I said, I need books. Hundreds of thousands of books were pouring from all over the world, coming, arriving in Mosul. They are all labeled “for Mosul Eye,” and the books would be immediately admitted. Someone sent us a container of 20 tons of books. The heritage of the city—which is the memory of the city, the most visible element of our identity—was almost completely demolished to the ground by the Islamic State, so we had to rebuild it. I started advocating with the world to help the city. Projects started working on recovering the Al-Nuri mosque, which ISIS had used before to declare its caliphate. Later, they destroyed it. We had to rebuild it. A church and a synagogue. And I have since been working on what I would call my life mission. Beside breathing life into the soul of Mosul, I realized that it cannot be completed until I make sure the Jewish history of Mosul, that was completely erased and omitted, goes back to the city itself. And this is why I began since then—I’ve been working on this in the past years, and still documenting the testimonies of the last people who were born Jewish in Mosul, who are still alive. Preserving the Jewish heritage of Mosul, but also not doing it in isolation; making it an integral part of the city’s history, so people will understand that they have a collective identity, a collective memory. I did not stop working on doing the research on extremism and terrorism. I did not stop working—I completed my dissertation in the past 10 years or so. I have been doing everything, David, dedicating all my time for the city of Mosul. I’m not going to list things, but I’m going to say what my life was: is that I was a person on a mission. And still I am, to help the city of Mosul recover. Whether it’s the same city I am talking about or it’s a different city now, it’s a city that deserves to live. Frum: [Novelist] Milan Kundera spoke of the struggle for freedom as being a struggle for memory and against forgetting. And you’ve talked very powerfully about the work of memory, what you’re trying to remember. The names and lives of people who were killed, the names and lives of people who were sexually abused. The city that is gone, the pre-city, or the older city that used to be there. Let us talk a little bit now about forgetting. Because the way you and I made contact in the first place was I had spoken about this terrible simplification that has been happening across the Middle East, where ancient communities have, one by one, been expelled. The Middle East is becoming a region that was divided into so many different religions and so many different languages and so many different ways of life. Unless, like the Jews in Israel, they can find their own state, there is no survival for them in this region in this terrible simplification. And there’s a forgetting of what the Middle East was. Can you talk a little bit about, as a historian of Ottoman Iraq and of Ottoman Mosul, what was there before? What was lost? And is there any way to recover that tolerance, that living together that was there before? Mohammed: I think it’s conditional. There is also, as you mentioned, there is a simplification of how the past looked like. There is a simplification of multiple definitions, including tolerance and coexistence. People assume that societies in the Middle East have lived, before even it was called Middle East, have lived in coexistence in a state of tolerance, and that is not the case. We’ve always been through this type of on-and-off situation. When the government has no interest in attacking the non-Muslims, including the Ottoman Empire back then, people are going to be okay. They are living their life, going on in their life, and that’s it. Whenever there is a problem, it will be immediately—it depends on the context—it will be immediately blamed on either the Jews or the Christians. But there is—in the middle of all of that, David, I’m not going to dismiss the reality. I’m not going to dismiss the fact that people have developed a model that allowed them to live in a coherent life, in a much more calmer life. But [it] was conditional with the fact that they had a space, and they had a place to communicate. And that was the market; simply the market. Because everyone who tells you that people lived in coexistence in their neighborhoods, that’s not true. In fact, the people did not communicate with each other in their residential areas. But they would always come together, and they would work, in the old markets: in a trade, in crafts. It even allowed the city to develop its own vocabularies and language, and allowed the people to work together, to live together, to contribute to the way of life together. However, it has always been fragile, because that social contract has never been strengthened, has never been made sustainable. It will immediately break down whenever there is an issue, whenever there is a problem, whether it’s an internal or external. Whenever there is—there is always this labeling of a treacherous people or disloyal people. As long as you are not religiously part of that faith, then you have the potential of working against the nation. There were moments in that history when things were much better. And that is during the period of what was known as, I think in the 17th through the mid of the 18th century, is “the phase of the city-states.” Meaning a family was in control of Mosul. There was the Jalili family, for example, for over two centuries in control of the city. He would have his most trusted minister in his cabinet as a Jew, and the other one is a Christian. His envoy to the Ottoman Empire was, in fact, Jewish. People lived in harmony. People lived in coexistence. But then when that condition ended, it went back to the same situation. Jews had never had the possibility to have a school in Mosul until as late as [the 1920s], until after the fall of the Ottoman Empire. Modernity came. And we understood—and this is to put it bluntly, brutally honest like that—democracy and separation of religion and the state have proven to be the only way for minorities to survive. And for people to understand that there is a way of life that is beyond history itself, that is beyond the promised caliphate, that is beyond these dangerous concepts that have been put in place for decades. It’s a complicated history. Cannot be simplified simply by saying people have lived happily in coexistence—because it could be one year of coexistence and next year a bloody year on people, and so on. This is why it was easy, for example—we have witnessed the collapse of that system immediately after the Islamic State took control of the city. It completely collapsed. That social contract completely collapsed. We’ve seen neighbors killing or raping their neighbors, the Yazidis, kidnapping their women. We’ve seen Christian people being expelled, and some of their neighbors would steal and loot their belongings. What type of coexistence was that? It was always conditional with—you need a strong state, you need good governance. But you also need a system that is not built on the infrastructure of religion, or the idea that Muslims are the majority, so they should rule and everyone should come under their control. Because that should not be the case. That should not be the situation. And it’s a complicated history also, because we still have conflicts we have not processed. We still have not asked the difficult questions. And David, I think I’ve already told you that some people have to get into the mud of that question and start facing them and start answering them. People have always been asking the question, How could we live together? How could we continue to live together? But these questions always get faced with punishment, because it also has become easier to say and to simplify, Well, it’s a diverse region. It’s a beautiful, beautiful diversity. People have lived with each other. How did they live with each other? Nobody asks these questions. And I think it’s the region in the world that is becoming less diverse. A region that’s becoming less diverse. You go to Iraq today; you can easily notice: This part of the country is Shia, the other part is Sunni, the other part is Kurd . And where are the Christians? Where are the Yazidis? Where are the Jews in the middle of all of that? This is a region that still needs some more work by its own people. I think people have to get things into their hands, matters into their hands, by facing the difficult questions. By facing the reality. For example, one of the outstanding questions: Why did ISIS happen? Why did ISIS took control of third of the country? Before that, why did Al-Qaeda even come to being? Why did people join the Islamic State? Why do people still have interest in something called caliphate in today’s modernity, in today’s fast-moving humanity? Why do you think people need a caliphate? I think these questions need to be asked. There is nothing wrong about asking them. There is nothing directed against a religion when we ask these questions. But when certain religions, when certain texts become the source for people like the Islamic State, I think everyone has the right to ask: What’s wrong with that? What’s going wrong? Frum: And when they ask, they will have your extraordinary work of witness and testimony as a guide to their better thinking. And maybe—possibly, let’s hope—to a better, more liberal, more democratic future. Omar Mohammed, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. Mohammed: David, thank you very much. And it was a little bit emotional for me. I apologize for that. Frum: It was emotional for everyone. Thank you. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Omar Mohammed for talking today about his powerful book, Mosul Eye . I don’t know how to make a transition to another book talk after that discussion. So I’m going to talk about something really quite completely different, which is not only not a book but an entirely different art form: opera. I went to see this past weekend the production of La bohème by Puccini at New York’s Metropolitan Opera. This is a 2026 production, but it’s a revival of an older design by the great designer [Franco] Zeffirelli. It’s a quite legendary production. The costumes and sets are in the basement. The most famous scene, that I’d heard about all my life and wanted to see in person, was at Act Two—which is set in a café, and suddenly the curtain rises on a Paris street. And there are rooftops, and there’s an open café, and there are hundreds of choristers and children. There are even a couple of live animals, a donkey and a horse, all of them reenacting what the Latin Quarter would’ve looked like in the reign of King Louis Philippe, which is when La bohème is set, although it’s written half a century later. I found myself thinking less about Puccini and less about La bohème than about the whole strange institution of opera. In any major Western city, there will be, probably, an opera house. And the opera house, it will be one of many theaters and venues, but it is usually one with a certain kind of statement of importance and formality. There may be sport centers that are bigger, but they’re never as central. And there may be theaters that are almost as central, but they’re never as big. And there’s always something about the opera that sets itself apart. Often, typically, it’s on a square, not facing the street. That’s how it is in Paris; that’s how it is in Vienna. And of course, that’s how it is in New York, where there’s this kind of formation of three buildings that set back from the street with a giant plaza in between. There’s a statement of importance. And people recognize this importance, and act on it. Very few people—almost nobody dresses up anymore to go to the theater. But people still dress up, especially women, to go to the opera. As I looked around myself, I saw women in long dresses, women wearing costume clothing that was quite different from what they’d wear not only during the day, but really to almost any other kind of evening out. And I thought about the kind of cultural knowledge that is embedded in this strange institution, and at the cultural self-confidence it takes to put such a building on such a square in such a city, and to summon people and to say, This is something that is different, not only from other things that you do during your everyday life. This is different even from other forms of art. This is somehow higher and more important and different and more formal. More commanding; more central. And I wonder: Where do people get that confidence? Where do people get that nerve? And then I found myself thinking: Do we still have it? Opera is kind of an ossified form. I mean, there are new operas written, but they tend not to be very popular. And it is Puccini and Verdi, and especially La bohème . La bohème seems to be the most popular opera, at least in the Metropolitan Opera’s repertoire, and this particular design has been played again and again and again. So it’s kind of an ossified form. And I wonder if the confidence behind that form is also becoming ossified too. Now, I’m not going to make a brief for opera. You may like it; you may not. You may want to see the show, you may not. That’s not what I’m interested in. What I’m interested in is: Can we still summon the cultural self-confidence to say, of certain kinds of works of art: These are important. These are things that people should value. These are things, whether you like it yourself or not, they have a central place in your culture and your society. And the texture of your city will endorse this idea, whether or not you have ever set foot yourself inside the venue in which this cultural confidence is expressed. And I think there will be critics who will say that kind of cultural confidence is misplaced. What about other things that other people do? Who’s to say? Who’s to say why someone has the authority to proclaim this and not that? But maybe we can’t get along without it either. Anyway, that’s what I was thinking about on my way in and out to watch Zeffirelli’s donkeys and horses in his extraordinary setting of this amazing piece of art, in this amazing venue in this great city. Thanks so much for joining me this week on The David Frum Show. It would be a great help to spreading the word of the show if you would share, subscribe, like on whatever platform you use. As always, the best way to support the work of this program and all of us at The Atlantic is by subscribing to The Atlantic . I hope you’ll please consider doing that. Thanks so much for watching and listening. See you next week on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye. [ Music ]

items.title: Aucun gagnant clair en Israël : après les élections, vers de longues négociations ?
items.description: Plus de 85 % des bulletins des élections législatives israéliennes qui se sont tenues hier, mardi 27 octobre, ont été dépouillés ce mercredi 28 à 17h (heure de Paris). Le bloc du Premier ministre Benyamin Netanyahou devrait recueillir 53 sièges à la Knesset (contre 64 en 2022), et celui de son principal opposant, Gadi Eisenkot, 48 sièges. Les résultats pourraient continuer d’évoluer d’ici jeudi. La commission électorale a jusqu’au 4 novembre pour communiquer les résultats officiels au président Herzog. Le scrutin est une victoire en demi-teinte pour le Likoud, le parti de Netanyahou, qui devrait terminer en tête avec près de 21 % des voix. Yashar !, le parti d’Eisenkot, est crédité à ce stade d’environ 16 % des voix, et la Liste unifiée, qui regroupe trois partis à dominante arabe (Hadash, Balad et Ta’al), de plus de 9 %. Il s’agirait de la meilleure performance de la liste depuis 2020, lorsqu’elle incluait encore Ra’am. Avec les 7 sièges de Ra’am, les partis arabes totaliseraient 19 sièges. Faute de majorité claire pour les deux principaux blocs – 61 sièges sont nécessaires pour disposer de la majorité à la Knesset –, les partis arabes pourraient être amenés à jouer un rôle déterminant. Plusieurs semaines pourraient toutefois être nécessaires pour tenter de former une coalition, période au cours de laquelle la situation en Israël et dans la région pourrait évoluer, notamment vis-à-vis de l’Iran et des États-Unis. Netanyahou a tenté de raviver la guerre avec Téhéran une semaine avant le scrutin, en envoyant des dizaines d’avions jusqu’à la frontière iranienne, dans une manœuvre qui aurait pu conduire à une riposte iranienne. Donald Trump, auprès de qui le Premier ministre israélien s’est tourné ces dernières semaines pour tenter d’obtenir des marques de soutien, s’est attribué mercredi 28 le mérite de la performance de Netanyahou. Dans une publication sur Truth Social, le président américain a relayé une déclaration attribuée à un certain Irving C. Schwartz : « Lorsque le président Trump a apporté son soutien à Bibi Netanyahou, le vent a complètement tourné, et aujourd’hui, plutôt qu’une défaite cuisante pour un grand Premier ministre, on semble assister à une remontée spectaculaire qui aboutit à une impasse, voire à une VICTOIRE pour Netanyahou ». Publication de Donald Trump sur son réseau Truth Social, le 28 octobre 2026. En Israël, le président joue un rôle institutionnel dans la formation du gouvernement. C’est auprès de lui que les responsables des partis politiques émettront des « recommandations » pour désigner la personnalité chargée de former un gouvernement, qui n’est pas nécessairement le chef du premier parti. Celle-ci disposera alors de 28 jours pour tenter d’obtenir une majorité, avec la possibilité d’étendre cette période de 14 jours. Si cette première tentative échoue, le président pourra désigner un deuxième candidat, qui disposera de 28 jours, sans possibilité de prolongation. Herzog pourrait confier ce mandat à Netanyahou, dont le parti devrait arriver en tête du scrutin. Tous les partis d’opposition ont toutefois exclu de gouverner sous sa direction, ce qui compliquerait l’exercice de formation d’une coalition. Il pourrait également se tourner vers Gadi Eisenkot, dont le parti, Yashar !, deviendrait la deuxième force politique de la Knesset avec environ 21 sièges, derrière le Likoud (26 sièges). Eisenkot aurait toutefois besoin du soutien, explicite ou tacite, des deux formations politiques arabes israéliennes, sur lequel il a dit durant la campagne être prêt à s’appuyer pour diriger une coalition minoritaire. Même s’il restait au pouvoir à la tête d’un gouvernement de transition, Netanyahou pourrait faire face à une commission d’enquête d’État sur les défaillances ayant conduit à l’attaque du 7 octobre 2023, que la nouvelle Knesset pourrait chercher à instaurer. Selon Haaretz , dont les informations ont depuis été confirmées par le New York Times , le dirigeant israélien aurait été averti par le président émirati Mohammed ben Zayed dix jours avant l’attaque que le Hamas, alors dirigé par Yahya Sinwar, préparait une opération majeure contre Israël. Le bureau du Premier ministre israélien a démenti ces informations. L’article Aucun gagnant clair en Israël : après les élections, vers de longues négociations ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Climat et sécurité au Sahel : Le Burkina Faso passe à l’action pour sa stratégie nationale
items.description: Le Burkina Faso entend renforcer la mise en œ uvre de sa Stratégie nationale de sécurité climatique (SNSC-BF 2025-2029). Les acteurs de la sécurité et de l’environnement se sont réunis à Ouagadougou, le 28 octobre 2026, dans le cadre d’un atelier organisé par le Centre national d’études stratégiques du Burkina Faso (CNES-BF), en collaboration avec l’Institute for Security Studies (ISS). L’objectif est de traduire les orientations stratégiques en actions concrètes face aux effets du changement climatique sur la paix et la sécurité. Au Sahel, les températures augmentent à un rythme particulièrement élevé. Entre 1970 et 2010, la région a enregistré une hausse de 0,6 à 0,8 °C, selon les données évoquées dans le cadre de cette problématique. Cette évolution accentue la dégradation des terres, raréfie les ressources en eau et fragilise les moyens de subsistance des populations. Pour le Général de Brigade Aimé Barthélemy Simporé, directeur général du Centre national d’études stratégiques, la question climatique doit être abordée dans toute sa complexité. « Le changement climatique ne constitue pas à lui seul une cause directe de conflits, c’est plutôt son interaction avec des vulnérabilités préexistantes telles que la compétition autour des ressources naturelles, la fragilité des mécanismes de régulation de conflits et les difficultés d’accès aux moyens de subsistances », a-t-il affirmé. Cette approche souligne la nécessité de ne pas établir un lien automatique entre changement climatique et insécurité, mais de prendre en compte les facteurs économiques, sociaux, institutionnels et environnementaux qui peuvent transformer les pressions sur les ressources naturelles en tensions sécuritaires. À travers cet atelier, les participants entendent dépasser le stade de l’adoption des textes pour examiner les conditions de leur mise en œuvre. Il s’agit notamment de renforcer la compréhension commune des liens entre climat, paix et sécurité au Burkina Faso, de dresser un bilan des premières actions engagées et d’identifier les acquis, les difficultés ainsi que les besoins prioritaires. « Nous en tant qu'institution, c’est accompagner le leadership africain face aux questions de gouvernance de stabilité au profit des populations », Fahiraman Rodrigue Koné Les échanges doivent également permettre de recenser les initiatives efficaces et de partager les expériences susceptibles d’être reproduites dans d’autres localités. Cette démarche vise à améliorer la coordination entre les acteurs concernés et à favoriser une réponse adaptée aux réalités des communautés. La coopération entre le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger constitue un autre enjeu de cette dynamique. Le partage des expériences, des réussites et des difficultés rencontrées dans la mise en œuvre des stratégies nationales pourrait contribuer à renforcer les réponses communes aux défis climatiques et sécuritaires dans l’espace sahélien. « Nous en tant qu'institution, c’est accompagner le leadership africain face aux questions de gouvernance, de stabilité au profit des populations », a lancé Fahiraman Rodrigue Koné pour le compte de l’Institute for Security Studies (ISS). En misant sur une meilleure articulation entre politiques environnementales, prévention des conflits et actions de sécurité, le Burkina Faso entend ainsi faire de sa stratégie nationale un instrument opérationnel au service de la résilience des populations et de la consolidation de la paix. Grâce Kabré/Bazié , Elvira Fleur Bouda (stagiaires) Faso7 L’article Climat et sécurité au Sahel : Le Burkina Faso passe à l’action pour sa stratégie nationale est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Ogou: Une campagne de proximité de la CNDH pour sensibiliser les femmes sur les questions de santé
items.description: Atakpamé, 28 oct. (ATOP) – La Commission nationale des droits de l’homme (CNDH) des Plateaux-Est a mené, du 22 au 28 octobre, une tournée de sensibilisation dans plusieurs localités d’Atakpamé pour sensibiliser les femmes sur les questions de santé. La Commission s’est notamment rendue dans les quartiers de Campement 1, Djidja, Sada, Koréma et Kéta, ainsi qu’à la prison civile d’Atakpamé. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le cadre des missions de la CNDH, qui consistent à promouvoir et à protéger les droits de la personne humaine. Cette campagne de proximité a permis de sensibiliser les femmes aux signes d’alerte du cancer de seins, du cancer du col de l’utérus et d’autres pathologies ainsi qu’à l’importance du dépistage précoce. À la prison civile d’Atakpamé, les femmes détenues ont bénéficié d’un dépistage du cancer du col de l’utérus. En marge de ces activités sanitaires, les échanges ont également porté sur la responsabilité parentale, en mettant l’accent sur le rôle primordial des parents dans l’éducation, la protection et le bien-être des enfants. La responsable de la CNDH des Plateaux-Est, Mme Alliassim Falilatou, a souligné que la santé est un droit fondamental et inaliénable à chaque citoyenne, sans aucune distinction, qu’elle soit libre de ses mouvements ou incarcérée. Elle a exhorté les femmes à briser le tabou entourant ces maladies et à adopter les bons réflexes en matière de prévention et de consultation médicale régulière. La surveillante de l’administration pénitentiaire, Tchabana Aïda, a indiqué que cette action de sensibilisation constitue un réconfort et un accompagnement sanitaire précieux pour les détenues, contribuant ainsi à la préservation de leur santé et à leur réinsertion dans la dignité. Au terme de cette campagne, les participantes se sont engagées à relayer les messages reçus auprès de leurs familles et des communautés respectives. ATOP/KKT/MD

Others across the Middle East were merely filled with more pessimism after a nationalist veteran prime minister and a former hawkish military chief competed for Israel's leadership.

items.title: Guinée : 64 000 matricules fictifs débusqués, 643 milliards de GNF d’économies annoncées dans la Fonction publique
items.description: Le ministère de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique a organisé, ce mercredi 28 octobre, aux Chapiteaux du Palais du Peuple, un atelier de restitution des textes et cadres organiques ainsi que du Référentiel des métiers et des compétences (RMC). La rencontre s’est déroulée en présence du ministre Faya François Bourouno, de son homologue chargé de l’Énergie, Laye Sékou Camara, ainsi que de plusieurs secrétaires généraux, chefs de cabinet des départements ministériels, conseillers, inspecteurs et hauts cadres de l’administration publique. Cet atelier avait notamment pour objectifs de présenter les résultats de la saisie des textes et cadres organiques, d’exposer la structure et les modalités d’utilisation du Référentiel des métiers et des compétences, puis de procéder à la remise officielle des fiches de poste et du référentiel aux différents départements ministériels. La cérémonie de restitution et de remise des fiches de poste a également été l’occasion de présenter « Founba », une intelligence artificielle conçue pour accompagner la modernisation de l’administration guinéenne. Devant un parterre de personnalités, Alhassane Bangoura, directeur national de la Modernisation, de la Transformation administrative et de la Simplification des procédures, et Karamba Guirassy, directeur général de la Fonction publique, ont présenté les résultats des travaux menés pendant près de deux semaines. Leurs présentations se sont articulées autour de cinq axes principaux, notamment la genèse des textes et cadres organiques, considérés comme le socle de la modernisation administrative ; les limites de l’ancien dispositif, notamment du référentiel des compétences datant de 1965, ainsi que les innovations apportées à ce document ; les missions de l’État, les domaines fonctionnels et les cadres communs regroupant les métiers correspondants ; l’architecture du nouveau référentiel élaboré au cours de l’atelier ; enfin, les outils disponibles et leurs modalités d’utilisation pour les prochaines étapes de la réforme. Selon ces responsables, la réforme engagée a notamment permis de mettre en évidence l’ampleur des irrégularités qui caractérisaient, dans un passé récent, le système de rémunération des agents publics. « Jusqu'à 64 000 matricules fictifs créés au fichier. On est parti de 168 000 agents de l'État à 104 000 agents de l'État avant les retraits. » Dans leur présentation, ils ont également affirmé qu’aujourd’hui, le système de rémunération repose davantage sur l’identification effective des agents de l’État, grâce aux opérations d’assainissement du fichier de la fonction publique, qui ont permis de réaliser des économies considérables. « Sur les deux années antérieures, 643 milliards d'économies réalisées entre 2024 et 2026. Case départ pour ceux qui connaissent le film : c'est pour savoir d'où est-ce que nous venons. Pourquoi on parle aujourd'hui de textes et cadres organiques ? Pourquoi on parle de référentiel ? Nous venons d'une fonction publique où, à la fin de chaque mois, des sacs d'argent fusaient de partout pour la paie des agents de l'État. Nous venons d'une fonction publique où la paie se faisait à travers les clés USB. Nous venons d'une fonction publique où une seule personne pouvait toucher le salaire de 10 à 54 matricules. Et même où une personne pouvait toucher 3 à 4 primes de transport, primes de logement. Nous venons aussi d'une fonction publique où il y a un potentiel de minimum 7 000 agents vivant à l'étranger. Nous venons aussi d'une fonction publique où la prime des enseignants est payée à tout le secteur de l'éducation. Ça fait pour l'État 88 milliards mensuels. » Poursuivant leur présentation, les responsables de ce département ministériel ont insisté sur les changements intervenus dans le dispositif d’identification et de rémunération des agents publics. « Aujourd'hui, nous sommes confortables. Pourquoi ? Parce que nous savons aujourd'hui identifier chaque agent de l'État à travers un biométrique facial, Iris, Empreinte. Et donc, nous pouvons dire que les effectifs sont écartés. L'assainissement continue. Mais aujourd'hui, nous payons les seuls agents identifiés. Et nous pouvons dire que fonctionnaire et contractuel réunis, aujourd'hui, nous avons 128 000 agents. Mais est-ce que c'est tout ? Nous savons dire aujourd'hui combien de personnes se trouvent dans le département de la Fonction publique, de du budget, des économies et des finances. » Les intervenants ont également souligné la nécessité de mettre en place une politique de recrutement conciliant les besoins quantitatifs de l’administration et les exigences qualitatives liées aux compétences recherchées. Cette politique doit reposer sur une approche prospective et une dimension économique. « C'est-à-dire si on ne sait pas dire dans dans un an, dans 2 ans, dans 3 ans, qu'est-ce que nous recrutons, quels sont nos besoins, c'est on passe à côté. Et ce n'est pas aujourd'hui parce que nous avons beaucoup de pressions et les recrutements souvent dans notre pays sont poussés par la pression syndicale, ça ce n'est pas normale. » Les responsables ont ensuite présenté le bilan de la validation des textes et cadres organiques des structures de l’administration centrale, mettant en avant les avancées réalisées et les dossiers qui restent à examiner à ce jour. « Nous avons pu valider 646 structures, c'est-à-dire les textes et cadres organiques en même temps de 646 structures de notre administration centrale sont validés, dont 395 services d'appui, 61 organes de cabinet et 286 directions et services rattachés. Voici un peu le bilan sur les 905 structures créées par le décret, nous avons validé 646. Il y a 426 textes et cadres organiques qui ont été validés dans les ministères qui sont passés devant la commission. Vous avez 220 textes qui restent encore à valider dans les ministères qui ne sont pas encore assez, donc le ministère de l'Industrie, le ministère de la Pêche, la Primature, c'est pour inviter ces structures à soumettre leurs textes et cadres organiques pour examen et validation. Parce que sinon ce qui se passe, dans vos ministères, si les textes organiques ne sont pas validés, alors les missions ne sont pas clarifiées. Vos agents ne savent pas qu'est-ce qu'ils attendent ou quels sont leurs apports dans les objectifs du ministère. » Prenant la parole à son tour, le ministre de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique, Faya François Bourouno, a salué le travail accompli au cours de cet atelier avant de revenir sur la répartition des effectifs au sein des départements ministériels. « Il n'y a pas un département, si je ne me trompe pas, qui a moins aujourd'hui de 600 agents à sa charge. Les départements les plus gros utilisateurs : l'Éducation, qui a aujourd'hui environ 49 000 agents que nous payons. Je crois que l'Éducation est suivie par la Sécurité, qui a environ 20 000 agents, et après, c'est la la Santé. Les trois départements réunis font à peu près 70-75 % de l'effectif global de notre fonction publique. La différence, c'est les agents qui sont répartis dans divers départements ministériels. Et si vous imaginez pour certains départements le nombre d'agents que nous payons à leurs comptes, on se pose la question : est-ce que réellement ce département avait besoin de cet effectif ? Je prends un département comme Économie, Finances, Budget, ce département a environ 1 300 agents aujourd'hui que nous payons. Alors la question : est-ce que le cadre organique qui exprime le besoin en terme de postes et d'agents rime avec cet effectif ? Ce travail nous permet de répondre à cette question », a-t-il déclaré. Revenant sur les déclarations répétées du président de la République concernant la place du capital humain dans le développement national, le ministre a rappelé que cette ambition devait se traduire par des réformes concrètes au sein de l’administration publique. « Il a voulu que cette conviction ne reste pas un slogan, et qu'elle s'inscrive au cœur du programme de transformation de notre pays, à côté du financement de la transformation locale, du contenu local et des corridors économiques. Or, le capital humain d'une nation ne se résume pas à sa jeunesse, à ses écoles et à ses centres de formation. Aussi essentielles soient-ils, il se joue aussi, et peut-être surtout, dans la manière dont l'État emploie ses propres compétences. Quel que soit le talent d'une génération, si l'administration qui doit l'accueillir est mal organisée, si les postes sont flous, si les carrières y sont aléatoires, ce talent, s'il y était, il s'éteint, mais également, il peut parfois s'enfuir. Voilà pourquoi la refondation de l'administration n'est pas un chantier parallèle au programme Simandou. Elle en est une condition essentielle, je dirais même indispensable du programme. » Dans les perspectives, le ministre a annoncé le lancement, à partir de janvier prochain, d’un vaste chantier consacré à l’évaluation de la performance des agents publics. Cette initiative devrait permettre de renforcer la responsabilisation des cadres et d’instaurer une culture du résultat à tous les niveaux de l’administration. « Notre souhait, c'est qu'en début d'année, chaque ministre assigne un contrat de performance à son SG, à sa cheffe de cabinet ou les membres de son cabinet, que le secrétaire général assigne des contrats de performance aux directeurs techniques dont il a la charge de coordonner, que le directeur assigne des contrats de performance au chef de division. Au-delà des contrats de service que nous signons aujourd'hui dont les structures sont responsables, il faut aussi individualiser la responsabilité, parce que chaque individu occupe une fonction. Donc l'évaluation de la performance va être un grand chantier que nous allons ouvrir dès le mois de janvier. Et ça va marquer aussi un changement de paradigme, parce que pendant longtemps, notre gestion du personnel a été avant tout une gestion administrative, c'est-à-dire un agent, un matricule, un dossier, un arrêté. Elle était nécessaire, mais elle n'est plus suffisante aux yeux du contexte que nous vivons aujourd'hui. » Le ministre a également souligné que cette évolution devait s’accompagner d’une transformation profonde des méthodes de gestion des ressources humaines, désormais orientées vers les emplois, les compétences et les résultats. « Nous passons progressivement d'une gestion des agents à une gestion des emplois et des compétences, d'une administration qui se demande qui occupe quel poste à une administration qui se demande quel poste est nécessaire, quelles compétences il exige et comment on y prépare, on y affecte et on y accompagne la bonne personne, d'une logique de moyens où l'on mesure ce que l'on dépense à une logique de résultat où l'on mesure ce que l'on obtient. Et ce chantier va rimer aussi avec la transformation ou la migration de la gestion budgétaire vers le budget programme. Dans le langage de la gestion des ressources humaines, on parle de passage d'une administration du personnel à une gestion stratégique désormais des ressources humaines. » En conclusion, Faya François Bourouno a appelé les responsables administratifs à adopter une posture davantage axée sur l’équité, l’accompagnement des équipes, la définition d’objectifs clairs et la reconnaissance du travail accompli. « Je demande donc aux responsables à tous les niveaux une posture tout aussi exigeante. Être cadre, ce n'est pas seulement signer et contrôler, c'est répartir le travail avec équité, expliquer, fixer les objectifs réalisables, accompagner, reconnaître ce qui est bien fait, corriger ce qui doit l'être. Le manager public est celui qui fait grandir ses équipes. Quant aux responsables des ressources humaines, le moment est venu pour votre fonction de prendre toute sa place. Vous n'êtes pas les gardiens de dossiers, vous êtes les ajusteurs du capital humain dans vos fonctions et dans vos départements respectifs. Et ces nouveaux outils vous donnent les moyens de l'aide, la condition de la réussite. » À travers cet atelier de restitution, le ministère entend ainsi consolider les bases d’une administration publique mieux structurée, plus transparente et plus performante. La validation des textes et cadres organiques, l’élaboration du Référentiel des métiers et des compétences et la mise en place de mécanismes d’évaluation constituent autant de leviers destinés à améliorer la gestion des ressources humaines et à aligner les effectifs de l’État sur les besoins réels des services publics. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Guinée : 64 000 matricules fictifs débusqués, 643 milliards de GNF d’économies annoncées dans la Fonction publique est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
